Recent findings suggest that we confirmed these findings using the complementary tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R clonal tracing model (Extended Data Fig. 11a–i). Whereas Cherry+ and Cherry+ Nr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC endothelial cells contributed similarly to arteries, eGFP-PIK3CAH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC cells were detected in 35% of arteries, compared with 10% for eGFP-PIK3CAH1047R cells (Extended Data Fig. 11c,e). Moreover, most eGFP-PIK3CAH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC cells that reached arteries did not form lesions, whereas eGFP-PIK3CAH1047R cells consistently generated small arterial lesions (Extended Data Fig. 11c,f). Nevertheless, eGFP-PIK3CAH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC cells continued to overexpand within the capillary plexus (Extended Data Fig. 11g–i). Together, these findings demonstrate that NR2F2 mediates the PIK3CA-driven block in arterial differentiation but is dispensable for mutant cell hyperproliferation in non-arterial vessels.

To investigate how PIK3CAH1047R activation induces NR2F2 expression, we analysed endothelial cells in culture. Nr2f2 transcript levels increased within 24 h after 4-OHT-induced recombination and remained elevated thereafter (Extended Data Fig. 12a). NR2F2 protein levels increased by 72 h (Extended Data Fig. 12b–d). To test whether Nr2f2 induction depends on PI3K signalling, endothelial cells were treated with the PI3Kα-selective inhibitor alpelisib (BYL719). PI3Kα inhibition reduced Nr2f2 mRNA and protein levels in a dose-dependent manner, accompanied by reduced p-AKT levels (Extended Data Fig. 12e–h). Similarly, alpelisib reduced NR2F2 transcript and protein levels in patient-derived endothelial cells with activating PIK3CA mutations (Extended Data Fig. 12i,j).

In a recent development, to investigate the transcriptional mechanisms underlying NR2F2 induction, we focused on FOXO transcription factors, major downstream effectors of PI3K signalling7,32, with FOXO1 the predominant family member in endothelial cells33. PI3K–AKT signalling inhibits FOXO1 through phosphorylation-dependent nuclear exclusion7,32 and, consistent with this, FOXO1 was excluded from the nucleus in vascular lesions of Pik3caH1047R mutant mice (Extended Data Fig. 12k,l). We next examined whether FOXO1 directly regulates NR2F2. Analysis of published RNA-seq, assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing (ATAC–seq), FOXO1 chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP–seq) and H3K27ac ChIP–seq datasets from human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) expressing constitutively nuclear, PI3K-resistant FOXO1(A3)34,35 revealed sustained repression of NR2F2 transcripts and protein, reduced chromatin accessibility at the NR2F2 locus and FOXO1 binding to a vein-specific NR2F2 enhancer (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 12m–v). FOXO1(A3) increased occupancy at this enhancer while reducing H3K27 acetylation and chromatin accessibility, consistent with direct transcriptional repression (Extended Data Fig. 12p).

Conversely, endothelial deletion of Foxo1 markedly increased Nr2f2 transcript and protein levels (Fig. 5h,i). Finally, induction of PIK3CAH1047R in HUVECs increased NR2F2 expression, whereas the PI3K-resistant FOXO1(A3) suppressed this response (Fig. 5j). Together, these findings establish FOXO1 as a transcriptional repressor of NR2F2 and define a PI3K–FOXO1–NR2F2 axis through which oncogenic PIK3CA disrupts arterial differentiation.

Using the vasculature as a model, we show that the consequences of PIK3CAH1047R are dictated by endothelial cell context. Depending on the differentiation state of the affected endothelial cell, the mutation promotes pathological proliferation, remains phenotypically silent or disrupts differentiation (Extended Data Fig. 13). This context-dependent model provides a mechanistic explanation for the marked predominance of capillary and venous lesions, and the rarity of arterial lesions, in PIK3CA-driven vascular disease. More broadly, it may also help to explain why PIK3CA-associated overgrowth preferentially affects mesoderm-derived tissues and suggests that similar principles probably apply to other pathogenic PIK3CA variants, which exhibit comparable lesion distributions in patients3.

Genetic lineage tracing revealed that endothelial cells expressing endogenous Pik3caH1047R persist in mature arteries without eliciting a detectable phenotype. Consistently, embryonic expression of Pik3caH1047R in Tie2+ cells does not give rise to arterial lesions32. This finding is unexpected given the broad endothelial expression of Pik3ca and the prominent role of PI3Kα signalling in all endothelial cells33. However, basal PI3K signalling is comparatively low in arteries and is not increased by endogenous Pik3caH1047R expression. By contrast, forced overexpression, enhances PI3K signalling and induces mild overgrowth in arterial endothelial cells that have not yet completed differentiation, suggesting that these cells require higher signalling levels to mount a pathological response than venous or capillary endothelial cells. Nevertheless, increased PI3K signalling does not induce overgrowth or NR2F2 expression in fully differentiated arteries. Likewise, reducing shear stress or Notch signalling, key pathways in the acquisition and maintenance of arterial identity30,34,35, does not restore responsiveness to Pik3caH1047R. These findings suggest that arterial endothelial cells possess multiple layers of protection that may also underlie their broader resistance to other mutations36. Future studies are needed to determine how microenvironmental cues, including extracellular matrix composition and mural cell interactions, contribute to this resistance.

Recent findings suggest that we also find that PIK3CAH1047R disrupts arterial differentiation at early developmental stages. During angiogenesis, a subset of tip cells acquires a pre-arterial identity by expressing canonical arterial markers (such as CXCR4, UNC5B, HEY1 and DLL4)30,37,38 and migrates retrogradely into nascent arteries to support arterial expansion. Pik3caH1047R disrupts this transition by inducing an early hyperproliferation response followed by Nr2f2 upregulation and loss of arterial identity. Supporting a causal role for NR2F2, Nr2f2 deletion restored the ability of Pik3caH1047R tip cells to contribute to arteries, consistent with previous studies demonstrating that NR2F2 antagonizes pre-arterial specification26. More broadly, our findings align with evidence that PI3K signalling promotes venous specification39,40, suppresses arterial differentiation41 and favours a stemness state42. Similar effects have been reported in other tissues, where PIK3CAH1047R biases ageing oesophageal progenitor cells towards self-renewal and induces dedifferentiation during mammary tumorigenesis14,15. In parallel, we show that proliferation blockade in Pik3caH1047R-expressing pre-arterial cells limits lesion formation, but neither reduces NR2F2 expression nor restores arterial contribution of mutant cells. These findings indicate that impaired arterial differentiation cannot be explained solely by proliferative exclusion43,44. Conversely, NR2F2 depletion did not block lesion growth or endothelial proliferation, despite previous reports implicating NR2F2 in cell cycle regulation25,45. Together, these findings indicate that PIK3CAH1047R-driven endothelial proliferation and the NR2F2-mediated arterial differentiation defect are functionally separable downstream outputs.

Sources indicate that our findings identify a transcriptional mechanism linking PI3K activation to NR2F2 induction. Previous studies showed that TIE2–PI3K signalling stabilizes NR2F2 protein during venous specification39 and that NR2F2 is elevated in PI3K-driven prostate tumours46. We show that PI3K signalling also promotes NR2F2 transcript and protein expression by inhibiting FOXO1. This is consistent with the established role of FOXO factors as nuclear effectors of PI3K signalling, including in PIK3CA-related vascular malformations47, and with the vascular overgrowth caused by endothelial FOXO1 loss48. Notably, FOXO1 has been reported to promote NR2F2 transcript and protein expression in pancreatic β cells49, whereas our data identify FOXO1 as a direct NR2F2 repressor in endothelial cells. Although the molecular basis of this difference remains to be determined, it is consistent with the context-dependent transcriptional activity of FOXO factors and NR2F2 regulation50,51 and may reflect differences in enhancer use and FOXO1 occupancy. Given that additional transcription factors regulate endothelial NR2F2 expression52,53,54, defining how they cooperate with or compete with FOXO1 will help to explain this context-dependent regulation.

Together, our findings show that the pathological consequences of oncogenic PIK3CA activation depend not only on signalling strength but also on developmental state and endothelial identity. Differentiated arterial cells resist pathological overgrowth, whereas pre-arterial cells undergo an NR2F2-mediated differentiation defect alongside increased proliferation. These functionally separable responses help to explain the vessel-type specificity of PIK3CA-driven vascular malformations.

Sources indicate that the in vivo experiments were performed in accordance with the guidelines and legislation of the Catalan Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock, Fisheries and Food (Catalonia, Spain), following protocols approved by the local animal experimentation ethics committee (CEEA) of the Institut Germans Trias i Pujol (IGTP) and local animal authorities of the State of Berlin (Landesamt für Gesundheit und Soziales Berlin). Mice were housed in individually ventilated cages under specific-pathogen-free conditions. All mice were crossed onto the C57BL/6J genetic background. Both male and female pups were used for retinal experiments.

The following mouse strains were used in this study. Pdgfb-creERT2-eGFP (pan-endothelial Cre line)55 mice were provided by M. Fruttiger. Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2 (pan-endothelial Cre line)56, Bmx(PAC)-creERT2 (arterial-endothelial Cre line)57 and Esm1(BAC)-creERT2 (tip-endothelial Cre line)58 mice were obtained from R. Adams. The R26-mTmG59 mice express membrane-targeted Tomato in the absence of Cre activity and this switches to membrane-targeted GFP expression after Cre activation, enabling cell lineage visualization and tracking. Pik3catm1.1Waph/+ mice, which harbour a Cre-inducible H1047R point mutation in the endogenous Pik3ca locus, were provided by W. Phillips60. In this allele, loxPsites flank exon 20, which is replaced after Cre recombination by a downstream version containing a CAT-to-AGG substitution at codon 1047. The two loxPsites are only 419 bp apart, making this region highly recombinogenic. Consistent with this, robust phenotypes are observed even at low doses of 4-OHT19. We occasionally observed vascular overgrowth in regions lacking GFP labelling, suggesting the presence of mutant cells in which the reporter allele had not recombined. Rosa26CAG-LSL-H2B-Cherry/H2B-GFP-2A-HAHuPIK3CAH1047R mice (hereafter iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R) overexpress the human PIK3CAH1047R cDNA along with H2B-eGFP-V5 (details are provided in the next section and Extended Data Fig. 5). The Nr2f2flox/flox mouse line61, provided by S. Y. Tsai, was used for conditional deletion of Nr2f2. The Foxo1flox/flox mouse line62 was used for conditional deletion of Foxo1. A list of all mouse lines and genotyping primer sequences is provided in Supplementary Table 1.

It has been revealed that to induce CreERT2 activity in pups, 4-OHT (Sigma-Aldrich, H7905) was dissolved in ethanol to prepare a 10 mg ml−1 solution. The stock solution was aliquoted and stored at −20 °C. Pups received intragastric injections in volumes adjusted to deliver the doses specified in the figures. To achieve the desired recombination pattern (such as sparse mosaic recombination, efficient recombination or recombination of multiple alleles), the 4-OHT dose was titrated for each CreERT2 line and experimental configuration (Supplementary Table 2).

To inhibit proliferation, pups received palbociclib (70 mg kg−1 in distilled H2O; Selleckchem S1116; intraperitoneal (i.p.), P3–P5) or mitomycin C (10 mg kg−1 in PBS, Sigma-Aldrich, M4287, i.p., P4–P5). To modulate blood flow and inhibit the Notch signalling pathway, pups received captopril (4.125 mg kg−1 in PBS; Sigma-Aldrich, C4042; i.p., P4–P5) or DAPT (100 mg kg−1 in DMSO/peanut oil; Calbiochem, 565770; subcutaneous, P4–P5). DAPT stock (10 mg ml−1) was prepared by dissolving 5 mg in 50 µl DMSO at 40 °C for 10 min and diluting in 450 µl peanut oil. To assess endothelial cell proliferation, pups were injected i.p. with 100 μg of EdU and euthanized 2 h later. EdU incorporated into the retina was detected using the Click-iT EdU Alexa Fluor 594 Imaging Kit (Invitrogen, C10339).

According to recent reports, to generate the iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R (Rosa26CAG-LSL-H2B-Cherry/H2B-GFP-2A-HAHuPIK3CAH1047R) mouse line, we introduced the DNA insert containing the H2B-eGFP-V5-2A-HA-humanPIK3CAH1047R gene by CRISPR–Cas9-mediated homologous-dependent repair, in the previously targeted iChr2-Mosaic mouse embryonic stem (ES) cell line31. To generate the donor construct of interest, we first obtained the HA-huPIK3CAH1047R sequence from the plasmid pBabe-puro-HA-huPIK3CAH1047R (Addgene, 12524) and cloned it into plasmid SO107 (Addgene, 99617)31, which contained the LoxP2-H2B-eGFP-V5-2A cassette. We then inserted the H2B-eGFP-V5-2A-HA-huPIK3CAH1047R cassette into the donor vector JP6 (Addgene, 99627), which contains the hygromycin-resistance gene. This resulted in the generation of the donor vector NA453, containing the complete donor construct of interest (Extended Data Fig. 5). ES cells of the G4 genetic background63 were cultured in standard ES cell medium consisting of DMEM supplemented with GlutaMax (31966-047, Gibco), 15% FBS (tested for germline transmission), 1× non-essential amino acids (Hyclone, SH3023801), 0.1% β-mercaptoethanol (Sigma-Aldrich, M7522), 1× penicillin–streptomycin (Lonza, DE17-602E) and leukaemia inhibitory factor. ES cells were maintained on dishes coated with a feeder layer of mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs). For each nucleofection, 2.5 × 106 ES cells were resuspended in 100 µl nucleofection solution containing 1.5 µg of circular px330 plasmid (NA505), encoding the guide RNA sequence (Guide3, GTTGCCTATGAGAGGCTAGAC), and 3.5 µg circular donor plasmid (NA453) containing the H2B-eGFP-V5-2A-HA-huPIK3CAH1047R sequence and the PGK-hygromycin resistance cassette (Extended Data Fig. 5). After nucleofection, 5 µl or 30 µl of the cell suspension was plated into separate wells on a six-well plate containing MEF feeder layers. Then, 7 days after hygromycin selection, 24 isolated ES cell colonies were picked for cryopreservation and subsequent screening. PCR with the flanking primers identified clones with correct homologous recombination and targeted insertion. After identifying correctly targeted ES cell clones, the functionality of the targeted allele was validated by transient transfection of a Cre-expressing plasmid. Positive clones were expanded and microinjected into C57BL/6J host blastocysts. Chimeric mice with a high degree of agouti coat colour were subsequently bred to achieve germline transmission of the targeted allele.

It has been revealed that mice were euthanized by decapitation, and their eyes were isolated and incubated on ice in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA; Sigma-Aldrich, 158127) in PBS for 1 h. Retinas were dissected and fixed for an additional 1 h in 4% PFA on ice, washed three times in PBS and incubated overnight at 4 °C in blocking buffer (1% BSA, 3% donkey serum and 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS) with gentle agitation. For NR2F2 staining, retinas were subjected to antigen retrieval by boiling for 20 min in 0.01 M citrate buffer (pH 6, Sigma-Aldrich, W305600) before permeabilization. Retinas were then incubated overnight at 4 °C with specific primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer. In iFluMosaic-PIK3CA retinas, the antigen-retrieval step required for NR2F2 staining abolished the GFP signal and prevented detection with anti-GFP antibodies; therefore, the retinas were incubated overnight with anti-GFP antibodies before antigen retrieval. After washing three times in PBST (0.1% Tween-20 in PBS), the retinas were incubated for 30 min at room temperature in PBLEC buffer (1% Triton X-100, 1 mM CaCl2, 1 mM MgCl2 and 1 mM MnCl2 in PBS (pH 6.8)). Secondary Alexa-Fluor-conjugated antibodies or isolectin GS-B4 (IB4) were incubated with retinas in PBLEC buffer for 2 h at room temperature or overnight at 4 °C. After three additional washes with PBST, retinas were flat-mounted onto microscope slides with Mowiol (Calbiochem, 475904), supplemented with the anti-fade reagent DABCO (1.4-diazabicyclo-(2.2.2)octane; Sigma-Aldrich, D27802) or Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech, 0100-01). For FOXO1/ERG co-immunostaining, an additional blocking step was included because both primary antibodies were raised in the same species, thereby preventing cross-reactivity. After the incubation with the anti-FOXO1 antibody and its corresponding secondary antibody, retinas were incubated with AffiniPure F(ab′)2 fragments donkey anti-rabbit IgG (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 711-006-152, 1:100) in PBS for 1 h at room temperature. The retinas were then washed, briefly fixed with 4% PFA, blocked again and incubated with the primary Alexa-Fluor-647-conjugated anti-ERG antibody. A list of all of the primary and secondary antibodies is provided in Supplementary Table 3.

Recent findings suggest that mouse endothelial cells were isolated from the lungs of adult mice (both female and male) aged 3 to 6 weeks. Under sterile conditions, lungs were minced and digested in 4 U ml−1 dispase II (Roche, 04942078001) in Hanks’ balanced salt solution (Gibco, 14170-112) for 1 h at 37 °C with constant agitation. Tissue was further dissociated by pipetting to obtain a single-cell suspension, and digestion was stopped with Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM; Corning, 10-013-CV) supplemented with 10% FBS (Biowest, S1810-500) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco, 15140-122). Cells were resuspended in PBS and incubated for 30 min at room temperature with rat anti-CD144 (Cdh5; BD Biosciences, 55289) antibody-coated magnetic Dynabeads (Invitrogen, 11035). CD144+ cells were washed in PBS containing 0.5% BSA and sorted by magnetic separation. CD144+ cells were plated on 0.5% gelatine-coated 12-well plates (Sigma-Aldrich, G1890) and cultured in complete DMEM/F12 (PromoCell, C-30140) supplemented with 20% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and two vials of endothelial cell growth supplement/heparin (ECGF/H; PromoCell, C-30120). Once confluent, a second selection with CD144-antibody-coated magnetic Dynabeads was performed for 1 h at room temperature. Cells were trypsinized, magnet-sorted, resuspended in F12 complete medium and cultured in a six-well format. Cells were maintained at 37 °C under a 5% CO2 atmosphere and used for experiments up to passage 5. Primary cells were not tested for mycoplasma contamination. Mouse endothelial cells used in Fig. 5i,j were isolated from Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2Foxo1flox/flox lungs as described previously64.

It has been revealed that to induce CreERT2-mediated recombination in vitro, mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R mice were treated with 5 μM 4-OHT for 6 h, with ethanol-treated cells as controls, and cultured for a further 72 h. Then, 1 day before immunofluorescence analysis, cells were replated at low confluency onto gelatine-coated coverslips in 12-well plates. At 4 h before collection, the culture medium was replaced with starvation medium, after which cells were processed for immunofluorescence. Pooled HUVECs were purchased from Lonza (CC-2519) and cultured in EBM endothelial cell growth basal medium (EBM, Lonza, CC-3121) supplemented with EGM endothelial cell growth medium SingleQuots kit (Lonza, CC-4133) and 10% FBS (Life Technologies). According to recent reports, subconfluent HUVECs were transduced with custom-made adenoviruses (Vector Biolabs) to overexpress constitutively nuclear human FOXO1 (FOXO1A3-Flag) or control (CMV-null) adenoviruses (Vector Biolabs, 1300). The CD31+ fraction was magnetically sorted, resuspended and cultured in 0.5% gelatine-coated wells in EGM2 medium (PromoCell, C-39211) supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin (EGM2 complete) at 37 °C and 5% CO2 until confluency. Cells were then subjected to a second CD31-based magnetic selection. Mycoplasma testing was not performed on primary cells. For the vascular malformation (VM) 64, we obtained from 1,572 reads, c.3140A>G (H1047R) with a 45.86% variant allelic frequency and for the VM90 from 461 reads, c.2740A>G (E545G) with 48.37% variant allelic frequency.

To inhibit proliferation in vitro, mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Pdgfb-creERT2Pik3caH1047R/+ mice were cultured for 24 h in DMEM/F12 supplemented with reduced growth factors (10% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and endothelial cell growth supplement/heparin (ECGF/H)) to limit baseline proliferation and achieve approximately 40% confluency. Cells were then treated with palbociclib (2 μM) or vehicle (PBS), followed 6 h later by the addition of 4-OHT (2 μM) or ethanol while maintaining palbociclib treatment. Cells were collected 24 h after 4-OHT treatment for western blot, qPCR analysis and flow cytometry.

Sources indicate that for EdU incorporation assays, EdU (10 μM) was added 2 h before collection. Cells were processed using the Click-iT EdU Alexa Fluor 647 Flow Cytometry Assay Kit (Invitrogen, C10634) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Data were acquired on a BD FACSymphony A1 cell analyser and analysed using FlowJo (v.10.1, BD Biosciences). Cells were gated based on forward and side scatter to exclude debris and doublets before analysis as illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 3.

Imaging was performed with Leica Stellaris 8, Leica TCS SP5, Zeiss LSM 980 and Zeiss LSM900 confocal microscopes, operated with LAS X v.4.8.2, LAS AF v.2.7 and Zen v.3.9 software, respectively. Adobe Photoshop (v.25.12.0), Adobe Illustrator (64-bit, v.29.0.1), ImageJ v.1.54b, CellProfiler v.4.2.6 and Imaris v.10.1 were used for image processing and quantification. All images shown in the figures are maximum intensity projections. Images were taken from at least three retinal areas in each retina and are representative of at least four retinas analysed for each genotype unless otherwise stated. The identification of retinal vascular lesions and their locations was performed by observing IB4 in ×10 images. Vascular malformations were defined based on abnormal vessel morphology and GFP+ clonal expansion. In capillary beds, lesions were identified as focal regions displaying abnormal vessel enlargement compared with the surrounding capillary plexus and associated clusters of GFP+ endothelial cells. In veins and arteries, malformations were defined by the presence of GFP+ endothelial cell clusters indicative of clonal expansion, together with abnormal vessel enlargement compared with control vessels. Retinal vascularity was measured using the IB4 channel by adjusting the threshold to select IB4+, followed by quantification of the percentage of IB4+ area relative to the total retinal surface. Vessel width was determined by measuring the average diameter at three different points along each vessel. GFP+ cell expansion was quantified by calculating the percentage of GFP+ area within the IB4+ area. For capillary analysis, images containing only capillary beds were used. To quantify GFP+ cells in veins and arteries, IB4 staining was used to delineate the vascular area, and vessel-specific regions of interest (ROIs) corresponding to arteries or veins were manually selected. For quantification of aEC-GFP+ endothelial cells, the analysed area was defined by a fixed ROI (200 × 550 μm (P6 retinas), 200 × 630 μm (P9 retinas) and 500 × 1,200 μm (P12 retinas)) to maintain consistent arterial length across replicates and to avoid including other vascular types. In P21 retinas, aEC-GFP+ cells were spread across various vessel types, so the ROI for quantification included the entire vascular plexus. To quantify vascular p-S6 intensity, a manual threshold was set to obtain the GFP+ area and define the ROI. The integrated density of p-S6 was then measured within the GFP+ area. In iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R mice, p-S6 integrated density was quantified separately in Cherry+ (WT) or eGFP+ (PIK3CAH1047R) cells after manual delineation of IB4+ areas containing each recombinant cell population. In both cases, the background signal (mean grey values) was measured in adjacent IB4-negative regions. The corrected total fluorescence (CTF) was calculated using the following equation: CTF = integrated density – (vascular area × mean grey background value). αSMA, CX37 and UNC5B expression in endothelial cells was quantified by measuring the mean intensity within GFP+ areas. Endothelial cell proliferation was quantified as the percentage of ERG+ endothelial cell nuclei co-immunostained positive for Ki-67 or EdU relative to the total number of ERG+ nuclei within the GFP+ area. In the iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R model, proliferation was quantified separately for Cherry+ and eGFP+ nuclei as the percentage of Ki-67+ nuclei relative to the total number of Cherry+ or eGFP+ nuclei, respectively. Nuclear FOXO1 positivity was quantified as the percentage of FOXO1+ERG+ nuclei relative to the total number of ERG+ nuclei within the GFP+ area. NR2F2 levels were assessed by manual scoring of nuclear immunofluorescence intensity in ERG+ endothelial cells. Endothelial nuclei with strong and unequivocal nuclear signal were classified as NR2F2high, nuclei with weak but discernible nuclear signal as NR2F2low and nuclei lacking detectable nuclear signal were classified as NR2F2negative, including after a substantial increase in display intensity during image visualization. Scoring was performed using identical acquisition settings across samples. Quantification of Cherry+ and eGFP+ endothelial cells in iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R retinas was performed manually, differentiating their presence in capillaries, veins and arteries. Vascular lesions were classified based on size as small (<10 PIK3CAH1047R cells), medium (between 10 and 35 PIK3CAH1047R cells) or large (>35 PIK3CAH1047R cells) based on manual counting of PIK3CAH1047R mutant cells. The incidence of arteries populated with PIK3CAH1047R cells was determined as a percentage in relation to the total number of arteries containing any recombinant cell. The relative arterial vessel width in iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R retinas was assessed by comparing vessel diameter in a central region containing recombinant cells with adjacent regions of the same vessel lacking recombinant cells.

According to recent reports, in cultured endothelial cells, maximum-intensity projections of confocal images were analysed using CellProfiler (v.4.2.6). DAPI, eGFP, Cherry and Ki-67 signals were defined as primary objects. Nuclei were identified based on DAPI staining and used to generate secondary objects for p-S6 quantification. CellProfiler assigned p-S6 intensity to individual nuclei and classified cells as p-S6+ or p-S6−. WT and PIK3CAH1047R endothelial cells were quantified by identifying Cherry+DAPI+ and eGFP+DAPI+ cells, respectively.

FOXO1-bound Nr2f2 enhancer identification was performed according an approach described previously67. In brief, enhancer marks from three published datasets were used to identify putative enhancers: (1) open chromatin as assessed by ATAC–seq in mouse P6 retina endothelial cells (MRECs)68; (2) enriched EP300 binding in Tie2-cre+ cells from embryonic day 11.5 mouse embryos69; and (3) binding of the ETS factor ERG, which marks all known endothelial cell enhancers, in HUVECs70. Putative enhancer regions were then assessed for FOXO1(A3) binding47,65, identifying the FOXO1-bound NR2F2-1345 enhancer. For in vivo validation, the NR2F2-1345 enhancer sequence was cloned into the E1b-GFP-Tol2-Gateway vector71 using the Gene Synthesis service from Genewiz (part of Azenta Life Sciences). F0 mosaic transgenic zebrafish embryos were generated using Tol2-mediated integration72. All animal procedures were approved by a local ethical review committee at Oxford University, licensed by the UK Home Office and conducted in accordance with ARRIVE guidelines. All zebrafish (KLC strain) were maintained in groups. Embryos were maintained in E3 medium (5 mM NaCl, 0.17 mM KCl, 0.33 mM CaCl2, 0.33 mM MgSO4) at 28.5 °C. To image, all embryos were dechorionated and anaesthetized with 0.01% tricaine methanesulfonate in E3 medium. For analysis of transgenic zebrafish, single embryos were transferred into a flat-bottom 96-well plate, mounted in 0.1% TopVision low-melting-point agarose (Thermo Fisher Scientific, R0801) in E3 medium with tricaine methanesulfonate (Merck, A5040). GFP reporter gene expression was screened with a Zeiss LSM 980 (Carl Zeiss) confocal microscope at 32–72 h post-fertilization. Whole zebrafish were imaged using the ‘tile scan’ command, combined with z-stack collection, at 488 nm excitation and 510 nm emission for eGFP.

To target tip endothelial cells, recombination was induced with 25 mg kg−1 4-OHT at P1 and P2 in Esm1(BAC)-creERT2R26-mTmG (control) and Esm1(BAC)-creERT2R26-mTmG;Pik3caH1047R (mutant) mice. Retinas were collected at P6 and processed fresh for enzymatic dissociation using the Neural Tissue Dissociation Kit (P) (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-092-628). After dissociation, the cell suspension was incubated with CD31 MicroBeads (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-097-418) and subjected to two consecutive rounds of magnetic separation using MS columns (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-042-201) and an OctoMACS Separator (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-042-109). Cells were resuspended in 0.04% BSA in PBS and processed for scRNA-seq using the 10x Genomics platform. Two independent experiments were performed on separate days using independent cohorts of control and mutant mice, with retinas pooled per genotype (Exp1: n = 5 control, n = 3 mutant; Exp2: n = 4 control, n = 4 mutant).

In a recent development, mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Pdgfb-creERT2Pik3caH1047R/+ mice were treated in vitro overnight with 2 μM 4-OHT to induce recombination and expression of Pik3caH1047R, while ethanol-treated cells were used as a control (WT cells for Pik3ca). The medium was then changed to F12 complete, and cells were collected 48 h post-induction. Cells were detached with trypsin, centrifuged, subjected to debris removal (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-109-398) and finally resuspended in 0.04% BSA in PBS. For the scRNA-seq, three independent biological replicates were pooled for each treatment condition.

In a recent development, single cells were encapsulated into emulsion droplets using the Chromium Controller (10x Genomics) with the 3′ Next GEM kit (v3 chemistry) or the Chromium GEM-X Single Cell 3′ Kit v4 for in vitro and in vivo samples, respectively. Libraries were prepared according to the manufacturer’s protocol, targeting a recovery of around 10,000 cells per sample. Sequencing was performed on the Illumina NovaSeq X 25B platform using 2 × 150 bp paired-end reads. Raw sequencing data were processed using Cell Ranger (v.7.0.1 or v.8.0.1) and aligned to the mouse reference genome (mm10) using the default parameters. For the in vivo datasets, raw UMI count matrices were corrected for ambient RNA contamination using CellBender (v.0.2.1)73. This approach models background RNA from empty droplets and infers corrected expression counts for cell-containing droplets using a probabilistic framework. Corrected matrices were used for downstream analyses.

According to recent reports, all scRNA-seq datasets (in vivo and in vitro) were processed using a unified analytical pipeline in R (v.4.2.2) with the Seurat package (v.4.9.9)74. CellBender output count matrices were imported using a custom function designed to read H5AD files in R. Each sample was initially processed independently. tEC-GFP and tEC-Pik3caH1047R samples were initially analysed separately to prevent the pronounced transcriptional changes associated with the mutation from dominating the global data structure and obscuring the physiological organization of the tEC-GFP retina. After independent quality control, dimensionality reduction and clustering, endothelial cells were identified within each genotype based on canonical marker expression. The endothelial subsets from tEC-GFP and tEC-Pik3caH1047R samples were subsequently combined and jointly reanalysed to enable direct comparison of endothelial states across genotypes while retaining an accurate representation of the WT retinal vasculature. Within each condition, control filtering was applied to remove low-quality cells and uninformative genes. Cells were excluded if they contained fewer than 250 detected genes, more than 20% mitochondrial transcripts or exhibited a complexity index greater than 0.8. Genes with zero counts across all cells were removed. Potential doublets were estimated using DoubletFinder (v.2.0.3) on a per-sample basis75. Although doublets were not removed from the dataset, they were excluded from downstream differential expression analyses. Data normalization was performed using Seurat’s NormaliseData function with the LogNormalise method and a scale factor of 10,000. Highly variable genes (HVGs) were defined based on the distribution of non-zero gene expression counts, selecting a threshold corresponding to the third quartile plus 100 genes. Data were then scaled using ScaleData, and then a principal component analysis (PCA) was performed using RunPCA. To correct for batch effects across biological replicates, datasets were integrated using the Harmony algorithm (v.1.2.3)76, applied to PCA embeddings. The sample identity (ID) was used as the batch variable, enabling alignment of cells across replicates while preserving biological variability. Harmony-corrected principal components were used for downstream analyses. Graph-based clustering was performed by constructing a shared-nearest-neighbour graph using FindNeighbours, followed by community detection with the Louvain algorithm implemented in FindClusters. To specifically analyse the vascular compartment, endothelial cells were identified based on canonical marker expression (Pecam1 and Cdh5) and computationally subsetted. A secondary, endothelial-focused analysis pipeline was then applied, including re-identification of highly variable features, normalization, scaling, PCA and Harmony integration76. Multiple clustering resolutions (0.1, 0.3 and 0.5) were evaluated, with a resolution of 0.3 selected as it best recapitulated known endothelial cell subpopulations (for example, tip, arterial, venous and proliferative endothelial cells). Cluster annotation was performed using a one-versus-all differential expression approach with Seurat’s FindAllMarkers function, applying the Wilcoxon rank-sum test and Bonferroni correction for multiple testing.

In the in vivo retinal endothelial cell dataset, GFP expression was used to identify recombined endothelial cells. To enable GFP quantification, the GFP coding sequence was appended to the standard mouse reference genome (mm10), and raw sequencing reads were aligned against this modified reference using 10x Genomics Cell Ranger v.8.0.1. This allowed simultaneous quantification of endogenous transcripts and GFP expression. To identify GFP-expressing cells, GFP transcript levels were examined across the dataset. Density plots of log-normalized GFP expression revealed a bimodal distribution, which enabled the application of a stringer classification threshold (log-normalized expression > 1.5). Cells with log-normalized GFP expression of greater than 1.5 were classified as GFP+, whereas cells with expression at or below this threshold were classified as GFP−.

Differential expression analysis was performed by comparing mutant (GFP+ Pik3caH1047R) and WT (GFP+ WT) cells within defined endothelial cell populations using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test implemented in Seurat (FindMarkers). To enhance robustness and account for sparsity inherent to single-cell data, a complementary pseudobulk approach was applied. Raw counts were aggregated at the sample level (grouped by ID and phenotype) using AggregateExpression, treating each mouse as an independent biological replicate. The resulting count matrix was analysed using DESeq2 (v.1.38.3)77, applying a generalized linear model based on the negative binomial distribution. Concordance between single-cell and pseudobulk approaches was assessed by correlating log2[FC] values across clusters and evaluating overlap of significantly regulated genes (adjusted P < 0.05). A high level of agreement in both magnitude and direction of gene regulation was observed. Based on this consistency, Wilcoxon-derived results were used for downstream visualization and functional analyses due to their higher sensitivity, while pseudobulk results served as an independent validation of biological signal.

Average expression profiles were calculated for each endothelial population using Seurat’s AverageExpression function and HVG. The 1,500 most variable genes were scaled by gene and hierarchically clustered using Pearson correlation distance and average linkage. Analyses included either all endothelial cells from tEC-GFP retinas, irrespective of GFP status, or only traced GFP+ endothelial cells from tEC-GFP and tEC-Pik3caH1047R retinas. In the latter, populations were additionally stratified by genotype. Heat maps were generated using ComplexHeatmap (v.2.15.4).

According to recent reports, to control for potential biases from unequal cell numbers between conditions (GFP+ Pik3caH1047R versus GFP+ WT), we implemented a bootstrapped downsampling strategy. For each endothelial cell subtype, 1,000 iterations of random subsampling were performed. In each iteration, the condition with more cells was downsampled to match the size of the smaller group, thereby generating balanced datasets. Differential expression was recalculated in each iteration using the Wilcoxon test (FindMarkers, with logfc.threshold = 0 and min.pct = 0). For each gene, the frequency of significance (adjusted P < 0.05) and the consistency of log2[FC] direction were recorded across iterations. This approach confirmed that the identified transcriptional signatures were stable and reproducible, supporting their interpretation as robust biological features of the mutant phenotype rather than artefacts driven by differences in cell numbers.

Industry observers note that the expression of Nr2f2 and proliferation scores across GFP+ WT and GFP+ Pik3caH1047R endothelial cells were estimated. Cell cycle and proliferation scores (the sum of S and G2/M phases) were computed using ccAFv278. Biological thresholds were established: the Nr2f2 threshold was set at the 99th percentile of reference WT arterial and artery capillary cells, and proliferation status used a cut-off of 0.1. Cells were categorized into Nr2f2 status, proliferation status and a joint status (double high, Nr2f2 high, proliferation high or low/basal).

RNA velocity was inferred with scVelo in GFP+ endothelial cells and further analysed using CellRank v.2. GFP+ WT and GFP+ Pik3caH1047R cells were analysed independently using identical parameters. For each genotype, 2,000 highly variable genes were selected, and genotype-specific neighbourhood graphs and expression moments were calculated using 30 principal components and 15 neighbours. Transcriptional dynamics and velocities were estimated using the dynamical model. CellRank was subsequently used to construct a velocity-based transition matrix using the VelocityKernel and to identify macrostates using GPCCA. Velocity vectors were projected onto the shared integrated UMAP and visualized as streamlines and cell-level arrows.

Statistical analysis was performed using Prism 10 (GraphPad). Data are presented as the mean ± s.e.m. For in vivo experiments, each retina was considered an independent experimental unit. At least three mice from at least two independent litters were used per condition, except for in Extended Data Fig. 11i (n = 2). For the iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R model, only retinas containing identified recombined cells were included. Experiments using mouse endothelial cells included biological replicates, whereas those using human endothelial cells were performed as independent experimental repeats. Sample sizes are indicated in the figure legends. Statistical significance between two groups was assessed using either an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests or the two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-tests. For comparisons involving more than two groups, one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test or two-way ANOVA with Šídák’s test was used. No statistical method was used to predetermine sample sizes; sample sizes were based on previous experiments. Reproducibility was confirmed through multiple independent experiments. The experiments were not randomized, and the investigators were not blinded during the experiments or data analysis.

a, Details of construct generation are provided in Methods. PGK-hygro-pA, resistance marker for selection; WPRE-pA, viral sequence that enhances transgene expression by promoting mRNA stability and nuclear export; CAG, strong and ubiquitous promoter; PGK-Neo-pA, resistance marker for ES cell selection; 2 A, viral peptide enabling equimolar expression of multiple proteins from a single open reading frame (ORF); HA, V5, and His, epitope tags for antibody detection; H2B, histone tag targeting proteins to chromatin; N-PhiM, non-fluorescent protein that is used as a reporter of promoter expression; INS, insulator sequence that prevents inappropriate enhancer-promoter interactions. b, Schematic illustrating the mouse strategy combining the pan-EC (pEC) tamoxifen-inducible Cre allele (Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2) with the iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R allele. c, Mouse lung ECs isolated from pEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R mice were treated with 4-OHT for 6 h, expanded for 72 h and then replated. Samples were collected at 24, 48 and 72 h after replating, following 4 h of serum starvation immediately before each collection. d,e, Confocal images of primary mouse lung endothelial cells (ECs) isolated from pEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R mice collected at 24, 48, and 72 h after seeding. Cells were stained with DAPI (blue, nuclei) and for eGFP (yellow, PIK3CAH1047R-expressing ECs), Cherry (cyan, wild-type ECs for Pik3ca), and Ki-67 (magenta, proliferating cells) (d) or and p-S6 (Ser235/236, grey) (e). f, Percentage of Cherry+ (cyan) and eGFP+ (yellow) cells among total Cherry+ and eGFP+ cells at 24, 48 and 72 h post-seeding (n = 6 biological replicates). g,h, Quantification of Ki-67+ cells (g) and p-S6 (Ser235/236) fluorescence intensity (h) within Cherry+ (cyan) and eGFP+ (yellow) cell populations at 24, 48, and 72 h after seeding (n = 6 biological replicates). Data are mean ± SEM. Two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparisons test (f–h). Scale bars, 200 μm (d,e).

  • An English soccer star has been killed outside a Mississippi taco restaurant just months after moving to the United States to chase his dreams.
  • In a recent development, krissh Mahatma, 18, was fatally struck by a bullet after a gun was fired outside the Green Ghost Tacos restaurant in Jackson at around 3:39 a.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By RICH JONES, US DEPUTY SPORTS EDITOR.

Published: 13:30 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 13:30 EST, 25 November 2026.

An English soccer star has been killed outside a Mississippi taco restaurant just months after moving to the United States to chase his dreams.

In a recent development, krissh Mahatma, 18, was fatally struck by a bullet after a gun was fired outside the Green Ghost Tacos restaurant in Jackson at around 3:39 a.m. on Sunday morning.

The London-born player was with teammates from his Co-Lin Wolves team when they came across a drunk man outside the restaurant, according to Dark Horse Press.

A fight broke out and a man pulled out a gun and fired into the group, hitting Mahatma, who was taken to a nearby hospital via a private vehicle where he died, according to Hinds County Coroner Jeramiah Howard, via WLBT.

Industry observers note that capitol Police have since arrested and charged Danny Luna, 22, with murder. The Mississippi Department of Public Safety did not elaborate on what caused the deadly confrontation.

'While this arrest is an notable step toward justice, we recognize that nothing can ease the pain of losing a loved one,' Police Chief Mark Miller mentioned, sending 'thoughts and prayers' to Mahatma's 'family and loved ones.'.

Mahatma, who played as a striker, was in his freshman year at Copiah-Lincoln Community College in Wesson, around 45 miles south of Jackson where the incident took place.

Krissh Mahatma, 18, was fatally shot outside a taco restaurant in Jackson, Mississippi.

Danny Luna, 22, has been arrested and charged with murder after the deadly confrontation.

He had made 14 appearances in his first three months with the Co-Lin Wolves, scoring one goal in September in a 3-2 win over National Park College.

According to recent reports, 'Copiah-Lincoln Community College is mourning the loss of freshman soccer player Krissh Mahatma. Krissh will be deeply missed by his teammates and the entire Co-Lin family,' Dewayne Middleton, the Co-Lin president, noted in a statement.

In a recent development, before moving to the US, he had played for Watford 'A' in the post-16 Community and Education Football Alliance league. Co-Lin announced his signing in February.

A fundraiser set up to support his family remarked he was 'just beginning a latest chapter of life far away from home' and added: 'his sudden passing has left his family, friends, teammates, coaches, and the entire Co-Lin soccer community heartbroken.

'Behind this tragedy is a family grieving the loss of their son and loved ones trying to make sense of a loss that feels impossible to put into words.'.

According to recent reports, the owner of the Green Ghost Tacos eatery mentioned: 'On behalf of the entire Green Ghost family, I extend my deepest and most heartfelt condolences to the family, friends, loved ones, and university community mourning the tragic loss of a young student. Our hearts are heavy, and our thoughts and prayers are with everyone affected by this devastating incident.

'While this tragedy occurred near our establishment, we would like to clarify that Green Ghost was closed and was not conducting business at the time of the shooting.

'The safety and well-being of our patrons, employees, and surrounding community remain a top priority. We are committed to cooperating fully with law enforcement as they investigate the circumstances surrounding this tragic incident.

'Out of respect for the grieving family and the investigation, we will refrain from speculating or commenting further on the details at this time.

'Above all, we recognize that a family has suffered an unimaginable loss. We ask that the community join us in extending compassion, prayers, and support to those affected during this incredibly difficult time.'.

Preparing for 45C: How Germany tests its crisis response

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine a situation in which prolonged drought has devastated Germany and much of Europe, taking a toll on people's lives, the environment and economy — with a heat wave with temperatures of up to 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit) compounding the situation.
  • About 180 organizations across Germany, including more than 60 ministries at the state level and nearly 20 federal authorities, are taking part in a major crisis exercise known as LÜKEX 26, which is built around this very scenario.
  • In a recent development, it is Germany's cross-government crisis management exercise organized by the Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance (BBK).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine a situation in which prolonged drought has devastated Germany and much of Europe, taking a toll on people's lives, the environment and economy — with a heat wave with temperatures of up to 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit) compounding the situation.

About 180 organizations across Germany, including more than 60 ministries at the state level and nearly 20 federal authorities, are taking part in a major crisis exercise known as LÜKEX 26, which is built around this very scenario.

In a recent development, it is Germany's cross-government crisis management exercise organized by the Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance (BBK). And it's been up and running for more than two decades.

The first LÜKEX in 2004 dealt with the scenario of an extreme winter with a major power outage. Lessons from that exercise proved valuable in 2005 when the Münsterland region of North Rhine-Westphalia — Germany's most populous state — experienced the worst power outage in the country's postwar history. When heavy snowfall caused power lines to collapse, leaving 250,000 people without electricity for days, there was a better understanding of who to contact and where the bottlenecks were.

Since it first started, LÜKEX has trained for scenarios involving terror attacks, an influenza pandemic, biological health threats, storm floods in northern Germany and gas shortages in southern Germany. The most recent exercise in 2023 simulated a cyberattack targeting government operations.

With the help of other ministries, the German Weather Service and the Federal Institute of Hydrology, the BBK developed a drought risk analysis to serve as the scenario.

Participants, which include aid organizations Malteser and the German Red Cross, didn't know the specifics of the challenges they would be facing until the exercise kicked off on Wednesday.

Industry observers note that at that point, they were told it was July 20, 2027. In that simulated future, they find themselves in a Germany that has been struggling with extreme heat for weeks; water levels in rivers are falling, food supplies are becoming scarce and emergency services are under growing pressure.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Patrick Pöhler, spokesperson for Malteser, noted additional details include supermarkets having run out of water, collapsed supply chains and skyrocketing prices to enter a swimming pool. He said the scenario also goes into how the situation is impacting sections of society.

"Emergency services and elderly care are areas that require particular attention," Pöhler said. "The increasingly extreme summers of recent years have shown how severely heat can affect staffing levels and operational capacity.".

In its scenario, the northern port city of Hamburg is tasked with managing the disruption of key transport routes that are impacting access to food and drinking water, as well as handling disinformation attacks that are fueling public fear.

"We have not conducted an exercise of this magnitude since the end of the Cold War. Yet such preparations are essential to strengthen our resilience and crisis-response capabilities," noted Hamburg's minister for the interior, Andy Grote.

According to recent reports, LÜKEX is designed to test and strengthen the country's ability to manage major crises at a strategic level. No matter the specific scenario, they all help test internal structures, workflows and decision-making processes.

"The lessons learned are continuously incorporated into improving preparedness, planning and cooperation in civil protection," mentioned BBK spokesperson Katharina Böcker.

According to recent reports, this year's topic was decided a long time ago, well before recent summers in which Germany experienced extreme heat, she added. Thousands of people died from heat-related causes during the hot months of this year.

"Crises such as extreme heat waves and prolonged droughts can affect large parts of the population and challenge the operational capabilities of our critical structures over an extended period," said Christian Reuter, secretary general of the German Red Cross, another organization taking part.

Observers take note of how organizations react in the crisis scenario to find out what went well and where things didn't run smoothly.

"We are explicitly encouraged to make mistakes," mentioned Malteser's Pöhler, because that is how weaknesses can be identified and addressed.

A first internal debrief is scheduled for Friday, he added.

A preliminary report with the main findings and respective recommendations is due to be published in the first quarter of next year. A full evaluation report will then be released later in the third quarter of 2027.

By BOBBY MANZI, FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 04:50 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 14:13 EST, 25 November 2026.

Former England football star Raheem Sterling avoided prison for dangerous driving and possession of nitrous oxide after it was revealed he spent 12 days in rehab.

The 31-year-old was handed a 12-month sentence, suspended for 18 months, at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court today and has been banned from driving for two years.

He was also ordered to complete 100 hours of community service and must pay a victim surcharge of £187 as well as prosecution costs of £85.

Sterling – who is currently without a club but has played for Liverpool, Manchester City and Chelsea – pleaded guilty after crashing his £270,000 Lamborghini Urus SUV on May 28 while under the influence of laughing gas.

Four police forces received reports about the footballer's dangerous driving before he eventually crashed his car into a metal gate on the A327 in Hampshire during rush hour on the morning of May 28.

Sterling told police he had 'a problem' with laughing gas after subjecting rush hour motorists to a terrifying 90 minutes of dangerous driving, in which he zig-zagged on the M3 and M25 motorways before swerving onto a slip road and crashing into a metal gate. Police found six canisters of nitrous oxide in his car.

Raheem Sterling is pictured leaving Basingstoke Magistrates' Court on Wednesday, shaking hands with his solicitor Leo Martin - he avoided prison time.

Sterling is seen after being pulled over by police earlier this year while under the influence of laughing gas in his Lamborghini - he later spent 12 days in rehab.

In the police station, Sterling was asked to judge 30 seconds with his eyes closed but was so impaired that he recorded 52.

The footballer – who wore trainers, a black quarter-zip jumper with a white t-shirt and black trousers – froze as he waited for the judge to enter the court room.

He sat with his back against the wall in the glass dock and kept eye contact with her while she read her sentencing remarks.

District Judge Kirsty Allman revealed that Sterling sought addiction treatment on June 15 and went into rehab for 12 days.

She explained that nitrous oxide had 'become a maladaptive coping mechanism during a difficult period in his career', adding that he was a 'role model'.

While his sentence does not mandate therapeutic intervention, the lead therapist at Banbury Lodge – where Sterling checked in – feels further treatment would be 'beneficial'.

His MBE, charitable work and time spent in rehabilitation were cited as mitigating factors, helping him avoid a prison sentence.

Allman added: 'You are 31 years old and a man of previous good character. I accept your character has been positively exemplary.

Sterling leaves the court with his solicitor having been given a suspended sentence.

Image issued by the Crown Prosecution Service demonstrates the damage to the Lamborghini Urus being driven by Sterling.

'(But) these offences are so serious that neither a fine nor a community order can be justified. The custodial threshold is clearly crossed, and custody is unavoidable.'.

However, custody was avoided because the law was changed in March 2026, with custodial sentences of one year or less presumed to be suspended – unless there are specific aggravating features – because of the overcrowded prison population.

Temporary chief inspector Chris Sharland of Hampshire Police said: 'Nitrous oxide, commonly known as laughing gas or NOS, is a Class C drug, and driving whilst under its influence is an emerging threat to the safety of motorists on our roads.

'Driving whilst impaired with nitrous oxide can cause unconsciousness, and in the worst-case scenarios neurological damage or death, so there is a very real risk of causing serious harm to yourself or other motorists.

'We urge drivers to be aware of not only the law, but the risk this type of behaviour carries – one decision can have devastating consequences.'.

In his pre-sentencing remarks, Sterling's lawyer, Jason Bartfeld KC, said Sterling is 'more concerned not by damage to his reputation' but the 'consequences' it has had for his family, particularly his children.

He added: 'Mr Sterling recognised the various unhealthy coping mechanisms that brought him to this position and has sought to address these in the most positive and effective way and with some success.

'All of it makes it extremely sad and a matter of his own personal regret, tarnishing his own personal reputation.

'The end point of this is that he is absolutely determined that he will never appear before a criminal court again.'.

Police bodycam footage indicated the moment that Sterling was arrested with canisters and a deflated balloon on his lap.

An officer could be heard saying 'you can put that down' to the footballer after opening his car door.

He could then be seen taking the items from his lap and putting them behind his seat.

Sterling gets back in the car after his sentencing and is banned from driving for two years.

Sterling, who won the PFA Young Player of the Year award in 2018-19, was then read his rights while being arrested after being asked to put his arms behind his back.

There was a 40mph speed restriction on the M25 as he veered from lane to lane during peak travel time, with one witness fearing a ‘fatal collision’.

His arrest, near the Minley interchange, where the A327 meets the M3 in Hampshire, happened four weeks after he had returned to the UK following the end of an abortive attempt to revive his career at Dutch club Feyenoord.

Sterling, from Berkshire, pleaded guilty in September to dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen after a single vehicle collision at 8.45am on May 28.

During that hearing, Basingstoke Magistrates' Court heard that Sterling was so impaired by the laughing gas that he was unable to perform basic police station tests like placing his finger on his nose or placing one foot in front of another.

Barrister Simon Jones, prosecuting, noted of Sterling: 'He appeared to be quiet, withdrawn and lethargic and actively fidgeting.

In a recent development, 'Eye lids drooping consistent with fatigue or drug impairment. He said he was feeling very cold, despite this being in the middle of a heatwave with 33-degree temperatures.'.

The 31-year-old was charged with dangerous driving and possession of laughing gas after swerving his car on the M25 and M3.

Motorist Fiona Jennings told police she had looked across to witness the driver of the Lamborghini with a balloon in front of his face which was so big she thought it was an air bag.

It was so big that 'she had no idea how the driver would have been able to see the road ahead,' Mr Jones said.

Ms Jennings described Sterling's driving as 'absolutely horrendous' and expressed 'genuine concern that the driver may kill someone'.

Evidence previously presented to court suggested Sterling was also inhaling laughing gas while at the wheel of the Lamborghini a full seven hours before his arrest.

A concerned witness called police after seeing the driver of the same car entering a McDonalds car park alarmingly fast at 1.10am the same morning and seeing the driver holding up 'a pink, inflated balloon'.

By 7.45am that morning, another motorist concerned by the Lamborghini erratically changing lanes saw the driver placing a white balloon to his mouth and inhaling its contents.

For 30 minutes, that motorist watched the vehicle weave between the inside and outside lanes and come close to smashing into the central reservation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla owner Elon Musk said on Friday that the tech giant would scale down production of the Cybertruck at its Austin factory in the coming year.

The South African entrepreneur said Tesla would be scaling back production of his futuristic but often-mocked pickup truck and amping up production of what he hopes will soon become a fleet of fully automated taxis.

"Tesla will be winding down production of the cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk mentioned on his X social media site.

The announcement follows a bruising week for Musk amid the US midterm elections, where Republicans struggled despite his major donations, with his companies losing billions in value by market capitalization as investors sought to ditch stock.

Musk later responded to a complimentary user online who hailed the Cybertruck as the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made," and calling it an "end of an era" by saying: "True.".

For years he had poured much of his enthusiastic marketing zeal into promoting the Cybertruck, saying during the 2023 launch "finally, the future will look like the future.".

However the oversized body, straight lines and stainless steel and the post-apocalpytic vibe these created also met with widespread criticism and even mockery.

The electric powertrain was probably a barrier to sales in the US, by far the biggest pickup truck market, where Musk had hoped to take on some of the country's top-selling gas-guzzling vehicles like the Ford F150 or the Chevrolet Silverado and the Dodge Ram.

Meanwhile, the car's striking shape, weight and size made it impossible for Tesla to try to crack Europe, where electric vehicles are gaining a much larger market share.

Unlike in the US, EU safety regulations place considerable emphasis not just on people in cars in accidents, but also on the dangers posed to pedestrians who might be hit by a vehicle. That meant it was not possible for Tesla to register and sell the Cybertruck for road use in Europe.

Beyond this, the vehicle's size would likely have rendered it impractical and unpopular on many European roads, where space tends to be at more of a premium.

Depending how quick the wind-down proves to be, the Cybertruck's production run could prove shorter than its five-year R&D phase.

Given its longstanding issues meeting Musk's very public sales and production predictions, Tesla does not publish sales figures broken down by model.

But according to the automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the manufacturer sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down from 38,965 in 2024.

At launch in 2023, Musk had predicted unit sales nearer a quarter of a million.

For orientation, Ford sold more than 800,000 F-Series pickups in the US last year, a slight boost on 2024's numbers. These vehicles start at less than half the list price of a Cybertruck in the US.

The IPO for SpaceX this year revealed that Musk's second-largest firm was comfortably the biggest buyer of Cybertrucks in 2025. It bought vehicles worth $131 million and did not even enjoy a bulk-buy or friends-rate discount, paying list prices for the fleet.

The Cybercab is a vehicular element in Musk's bid to transform Tesla towards a organization focused more on AI and robotics than automobilies.

Rather than just featuring the self-drive or driving assistance programs that Musk has been championing for years, the Cybercab has no steering wheels, pedals or mirrors at all and is designed never to have a human in control.

Musk say the model will be the firm's main autonomous model and will supply a global network of Robotaxis.

Starting in the past few months, around 300 such vehicles have been registered and have started operating, on approved roads in the Austin area near Tesla's Gigafactory Texas. They're being added to the existing fleet of autonomous Model Y Teslas being used for the purpose, serving in an area known as a geofence of around 680 square kilometers (264 square miles).

Bruno Fernandes has been dropped for Manchester United’s crucial Premier League game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday.

Michael Carrick has taken the decision to drop the United captain to the bench in the wake of his public criticism on Wednesday following the shambolic 4-1 Champions League defeat to Como.

Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics and has now been taken out of the starting XI.

The move had looked likely with Carrick refusing to rule out stripping Fernandes of the captaincy when quizzed on the matter on Friday.

Carrick had responded to Fernandes questioning the set up and approach by suggesting tactics can go out of the window when players are unprepared to run.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Manchester United vs Bouremouth.

Industry observers note that united enter Sunday’s clash against Bournemouth in the grip of a deepening crisis. Wednesday night’s dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat to debutants Como extended United’s’ winless run to seven matches across all competitions - their worst sequence since 2015.

With just one victory from their opening seven Premier League fixtures, United are enduring their worst start to a top-flight season since 1986-87. Head coach Michael Carrick, a multiple champion at Old Trafford during his playing days, finds his position under severe threat, with reports suggesting another defeat could seal his departure. While both of United’s wins this season have come at home, they remain winless in their last three at Old Trafford. On an individual level, Bryan Mbeumo has offered a rare bright spark, scoring four goals in seven league outings while Bruno Fernandes continues to search for form, and the captain’s recent outburst only makes the atmosphere more febrile.

In stark contrast, Bournemouth arrive in Manchester brimming with confidence. Marco Rose’s side have enjoyed a flawless start to their inaugural European campaign, sitting joint-top of the Europa League standings after a dominant 3-0 victory over Ruben Amorim’s ten-man AC Milan on Thursday. That result marked a third consecutive home win and clean sheet, with Bournemouth outscoring opponents 8-0 in that stretch. Midfielder Marcus Tavernier has been instrumental, leading the club’s scoring charts with five goals across 11 appearances.

Bournemouth will feel no trepidation visiting Old Trafford, having gone unbeaten in their last six Premier League meetings with United (two wins, four draws). With Carrick desperate for a stabilising result and Rose’s side riding high on European momentum, today’s fixture carries significant stakes for both clubs.

Sustainable cement production via a liquid-phase pathway

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3414 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, slowing climate change requires overcoming inertia in political, technological and geophysical systems1,2,3. Portland cement manufacturing is among the most challenging industrial processes to decarbonize, yet it remains indispensable for building the infrastructure underpinning the low-carbon transition4,5. Here, building beyond the two-century-old conventional cement process6, we report a route that creates sustainable cement, by accelerating its reaction kinetics through a microwave carbon-plasma method, reducing the standard processing time from hours to seconds. Our technique generates localized temperatures up to 2,400 °C, sufficient to liquefy the raw materials. These liquid-phase reactions promote elemental mixing and solidification, producing reactive clinker phases. Our in situ transmission electron microscopy captures the early-stage cement hydration process in real time, revealing that surface disorder accelerates clinker reactivity by facilitating the dynamic nucleation and growth of hydration clusters. Beyond typical limestone and clay feedstocks, we show that hydrated cement paste from waste concrete can also be processed into clinkers, meeting ordinary Portland cement specifications. By coupling circular resource use with ultrafast electrified processing, our approach enables sustainable, low-cost cement production at scale.

Premier League officials are 'shocked and furious' after the FA overturned Manchester United defender Leny Yoro's red card at Liverpool - despite the competition's own independent panel unanimously backing the dismissal.

Industry observers note that daily Mail Sport understands that the Premier League's Key Match Incidents (KMI) panel has returned a 5-0 verdict in support of referee Sam Barrott's decision to send off Yoro. The panel also backed VAR's decision not to intervene. Their findings will be released next Wednesday.

But an extraordinary row has now erupted, with United celebrating a successful appeal while the Premier League and refereeing body Pro Ref stand by the original decision.

United appealed against the red card following Sunday's 4-0 defeat at Anfield - Mauricio Pochettino's first game in charge - and an independent FA regulatory commission, consisting of three former players, rescinded Yoro's one-match ban on Tuesday.

The Frenchman was sent off for bringing down Alexander Isak as he ran clear on goal in the eighth minute. United disputed the referee's view that the Liverpool striker would have got to the ball before goalkeeper Senne Lammens, having taken a heavy touch.

The FA panel appeared to agree, on the basis Yoro did not deny Isak an obvious goalscoring opportunity, meaning the Frenchman is free to play against Brentford at Old Trafford on Saturday.

Referee Sam Barrott demonstrated Manchester United defender Leny Yoro a red card vs Liverpool.

Yoro was sent off for this foul on Alexander Isak - but his red card was overturned on Tuesday.

Barrott and his on-field officiating team from Sunday are believed to be angry at the overturn.

However, top-flight officials are now understood to be demanding answers as to how this has happened, with Pro Ref chief Howard Webb backing his referees.

It has been revealed that 'That (the red card) was the referee's call, made on the field,' stated Webb. 'Then the VAR checks whether the decision made on the field was clearly and obviously incorrect - and formed the opinion it wasn't.

Industry observers note that 'I think by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving swiftly on towards that ball. The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it's a little bit debatable, I guess. Certainly not clearly wrong.'.

Recent findings suggest that united sources have branded this interpretation as 'totally wrong' and say it is a process error that fails to interpret the rules properly. They believe that the VAR audio proves there was no meaningful consideration given to challenging Barrott's decision.

United dispute that it was a subjective call and say that it can be proved objectively in a matter of minutes using data that Isak could not have reached the ball before Lammens, even at top speed.

The Premier League and Pro Ref did not comment.

Amid protests, France's rising debt costs threaten stability

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.
  • If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.
  • France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.

If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.

France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.

Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.

As a result, the French government must pay higher interest rates on its borrowing than Berlin. The risk premium over German government bonds, known as the spread, is now at its highest level since the financial crisis. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more in interest than Germany on 10-year bonds.

The spread acts as a kind of "fever gauge" for bond markets, explained Friedrich Heinemann, an economist at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW) in Mannheim.

"This fever gauge then forces a change of course. If the spread rises too sharply, France's financing conditions come under pressure, and anyone in France who needs a loan has to pay higher interest rates. Banks then get into trouble, and the crisis escalates further," Heinemann told DW.

"This could then slide toward a financial crisis, which would finally send a clear signal to everyone: Things cannot continue like this unless you are prepared to risk a genuine economic collapse," he remarked.

Landry Charrier, a researcher at the University of Bonn's Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies, however, does not expect France's debt-fueled spending spree to end anytime soon.

In a recent development, "French people are aware of the country's high public debt. But debt remains an abstract concept if its consequences are barely felt in everyday life. According to INSEE [the French national statistics agency — Editor's note], 56% of the population receive more in government benefits and services than they pay in taxes and social contributions. The majority therefore have a tangible interest in maintaining the status quo," Charrier told DW.

For more than half a century, France has regularly spent more than it collects in tax revenue. The last time it balanced its national budget was in 1974.

France last paid a similarly high-risk premium at the end of 2011, during the eurozone debt crisis. What is particularly striking is how promptly it has risen: Since June 2026, the spread over German government bonds has more than doubled.

In a recent development, the main driver is not so much the general level of interest rates. Rather, it's the growing risk premium investors demand in response to high debt levels, political instability, large budget deficits and the recent unrest.

In a recent development, the higher the interest rates, the larger the share of the national budget that must be devoted to debt servicing alone. France is expected to pay more than €79 billion in interest on its total public debt in 2026. That figure is projected to exceed €91 billion in 2027 and could reach between €125 billion and €132 billion by 2030.

These figures include the costs incurred by social security funds and local authorities. The central government's interest bill alone is currently estimated at €62.6 billion by the Agence France Tresor, a French Treasury agency.

In the coming years, France will have to refinance large amounts of outstanding bonds that were issued when interest rates were at historic lows. At the same time, the country's substantial budget deficit means it must take on additional debt.

The trend of rising interest costs is also affecting Germany. The ZEW's Heinemann has calculated that German interest payments are likely to increase sharply by the early 2030s.

"For the federal government alone, which has so far paid around €30 billion, the figure will triple within a few years as both debt and interest rates rise. And it won't stop there — it will exceed €90 billion. Reaching €100 billion in annual interest payments in the federal budget is then no longer far off," warned the economist.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In France, however, economic realities seem to have little impact on political debate. Both the far-right National Rally (RN) and the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) are campaigning on costly promises.

It has been revealed that RN leader Marine Le Pen, for example, wants to reinstate the retirement age of 62 while promising €140 billion in savings. Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI's leader, has even suggested that government bonds held by the French central bank should be "thrown into the fire.".

"Nobody will ever notice they've disappeared," he has claimed.

For Heinemann, this is "a good example of radical parties on both the right and the left simply telling economic fairy tales.".

Their common message, he mentioned, is that "there is a way out of this mess that requires neither fiscal consolidation nor painful cuts.".

Charrier is convinced that many French people have yet to grasp the seriousness of the situation.

"The euro has made it easier for France to access cheap financing and has long softened the pressure to adjust," he pointed out.

It has been revealed that "In the past, currency devaluations [of the French franc — Editor's note] made economic imbalances immediately felt through declining purchasing power and rising prices. Today, that warning signal is missing. This has created the illusion that necessary adjustments can be postponed indefinitely," Charrier said.

This article was originally written in German.
