Immunofluorescence analysis of ANXA1 and SNAIL1 confirmed the state distinctions: TGFβ1 alone induced SNAIL1 expression, whereas YAP activation increased ANXA1, but these states remained overlapping under single-treatment conditions. Only combined treatment produced spatially separated ANXA1high and SNAIL1high populations as quantified by signal anticorrelation (Fig. 5e and Extended Data Fig. 12c), recapitulating the in vivo patient distribution (Fig. 3c,d). YAP activation also triggered nuclear shape changes and loss of heterochromatin (Extended Data Fig. 12d–f). Consistently, reanalysis of the patient tumour spatial transcriptomic data confirmed that fragmented architectures showed reduced enrichment of heterochromatin regulators (Extended Data Fig. 12g,h). This was validated at the protein level by H3K9me2,3 immunostaining of patient samples (Extended Data Fig. 12i,j). Loss of heterochromatin was associated with increased nuclear circularity (Extended Data Fig. 12k), providing a mechanistic link between YAP signalling, nuclear shape and tissue architecture.

To determine whether these cell-state transitions were coupled to behavioural consequences, we analysed organoid dynamics. Untreated organoids displayed spheroid morphology with expansive low-level growth. TGFβ1 induced cohesive invasion without substantially enhancing overall net invasion, while YAP activation triggered dispersive invasion. Combined treatment further increased the prevalence of dispersive invasion (Fig. 5f and Supplementary Video 1).

Sources indicate that to assess the in vivo relevance of these behavioural changes, patient-derived organoids (line 2) treated with LATS inhibitor, TGFβ1 or both were orthotopically transplanted into the mouse colon by endoscopy50 (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 12l). Untreated organoids did not generate visible tumours, whereas all three treatment conditions did so with variable efficiency. Mice receiving combined YAP activation and TGFβ1 treatment generated tumours (Fig. 5h,i) and, as expected, YAP activation enhanced nuclear YAP in the transplanted tumours while TGFβ1 treatment enhanced SMAD2/3 activation (Extended Data Fig. 12m). Quantitative analysis revealed that the combination treatment produced the largest tumours and the only tumours that invaded the stroma (Fig. 5i). Consistently, ANXA1 expression was elevated in YAP-activated transplants but was highest in combination-treated tumours (Extended Data Fig. 12n), collectively demonstrating that cell state diversification drives tumour aggressiveness in vivo.

In a recent development, together, these experiments demonstrate that tissue architecture and stromal signals collaborate to drive cell-state diversification and invasive behaviour. Architectural confinement suppresses β-catenin signalling to promote regenerative SC identity, while soluble stromal signals enhance EMT features. The combination of mechanical, compositional and signalling inputs from the microenvironment drives diversification into distinct SC and EMT states and potentiates tumour invasion.

Identifying the mechanisms that drive intratumoural heterogeneity is central to improving diagnostic precision and treatment outcomes in CRC. We demonstrate that tumour architecture and associated nuclear morphology are strong independent prognostic indicators, and that these features co-evolve with cell states within individual tumours. Fragmented architectures specifically associate with transition from LGR5-marked adult SCs to a fetal-like/regenerative state linked to aggressive behaviour and poor prognosis8.

The prognostic power of architecture derives from its co-evolution with plastic, aggressive cell states. Chemotherapy, wounding, inflammation and mechanical damage are known to reactivate fetal and regenerative SC programmes in CRC34,51,52,53,54,55. TGFβ1 drives WNT independence and fetal-like lineage conversion in CRC organoids56, and fibrotic stromal stiffening promotes aggression across solid tumours57. Our data implicate compressive forces from stiffened ECM in distorting tissue geometry, inducing fragmentation and promoting adult-to-regenerative SC transition. The regenerative state emerges as a hybrid with EMT features that TGFβ1 and stromal signals further diversify into spatially proximal but transcriptionally distinct SC and EMT states, suggesting a continuum in which the balance of signals determines which state predominates. Coupling of this diversification to invasion explains the association between fragmented architecture and poor prognosis, supporting a model in which disrupted tissue organization and inflammatory signalling initiate a feedforward loop driving disease aggression.

Our image analysis framework, combining nuclear and epithelial membrane immunostaining with machine-learning-based classification, offers an efficient stratification strategy independent of mutational status, and suggests that quantitative architectural analysis could serve as a tractable proxy for tumour heterogeneity in clinical decision-making.

In a recent development, the study uses a previously described cohort58 comprising 1,342 patients who underwent resection for colorectal cancer at Central Finland Central Hospital between 1 January 2000 and 31 December 2015 and had adequate tumour samples available. Formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumour samples were obtained from the pathology archives of the Central Finland Central Hospital Nova, which covers all colorectal cancers diagnosed in Central Finland (the population of the area averaged around 270,000 during the study period). Associated clinical data were collected from clinical patient records by study physicians. Moreover, all tumours were previously re-evaluated for disease stage, tumour grade (WHO 2019 criteria), mismatch repair (MMR) status, BRAF V600E mutation status and the presence of lymphovascular invasion58. Analyses of this cohort were approved by the Regional medical research ethics committee of the Wellbeing services county of Central Finland (Dnro 13U/2011, 1/2016, 8/2020 and 2/2023) andthe Finnish Medicines Agency (Fimea, FIMEA/2023/001573). The need to obtain informed consent from the study patients was waived (Dnro FIMEA/2023/001573).

The validation dataset was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee at Helsinki University Hospital (HUS/1223/2021). Permission to use archive samples without informed consent was granted by the Finnish National Supervisory Authority of Health and Welfare (permit number Valvira Dnro 1004/06.01.03.01/2012) and the FIMEA Finnish Medicines Agency (permit number FIMEA Dnro 2021/006901). Final TMA blocks of duplicate 1.2 mm cores were made in TMA Grand Master (3D Histech). For spatial transcriptomics selected full tumour samples from the same cohort were used. The authors affirm that the study was conducted following the rules of the Declaration of Helsinki of 1975, revised in 2013.

In a recent development, collagen analyses were performed on a previously described cohort59 comprising an independent cohort of 1,011 patients who underwent resection for stage I–IV CRC at Oulu University Hospital between 2006 and 2020. The analysis was based on TMAs that included four 1.2-mm-diameter cores, two from the IM and two from the CT. Analyses of this cohort were approved by the Regional medical research ethics committee of the Wellbeing services county of North Ostrobothnia (37/2020). The patients gave written informed consent for the study. Final TMA blocks of duplicate 1.2 mm IM and CT cores were made in TMA Grand Master (TMA Master II). For this cohort all tumours were previously re-evaluated for disease stage, tumour grade (WHO 2019 criteria), MMR status, BRAF V600E mutation status, tumour budding based on the International Tumor Budding Consensus Conference (ITBCC) criteria30, and the presence of lymphovascular invasion58. CD3+ and CD8+ T cell densities were quantified separately in the CT and IM, converted into percentile values, averaged across the four resulting measures and categorized as low (0–25), intermediate (>25–70) or high (>70–100), following the main principles of the Immunoscore assay.

Immunofluorescence staining and imaging of TMAs was performed as previously described60 for pan-cadherin antibodies to label the tumour cells and their plasma membranes and the nuclear marker DAPI. Imaging was performed using the Zeiss Axio Scan.Z1 slide scanner, with each round of staining recorded as an independent image. The CZI image file contained up to five fluorescent channels. For the full tumour samples, the staining was carried out on the same slides as spatial transcriptomics, after the spatial transcriptomics analyses. To select ROIs for sample collection for transcriptome analysis, the slides were stained with Syto13, pan-CK (AF532), CD45 (AF594) and αSMA (AF647)A to visualize nuclei, epithelial cells, immune cells and stroma, respectively. Imaging of the staining was performed on the DSP instrument using 50, 200, 200, 200 ms on the FITC, CY3, Texas Red and CY5 channels, respectively. After quenching the signal, the slides were restained for the indicated markers and the signal was imaged on the DSP instrument. The single-channel images were loaded to HALO v.3.6 image analysis software for visualization, registered based on the nuclear signal and fused to generate a composite image with 8 markers (including the nuclei).

Multiplexed fluorescence immunohistochemical staining and imaging was performed in 4–6 cycles as previously described60 for two sets of antibodies, listed below, and the nuclear marker DAPI. After the first-round staining and whole-slide imaging, the fluorescence signal was bleached, the antibodies from the first-round staining were denatured and subsequent staining rounds were performed. Imaging was performed on the Zeiss Axio Scan.Z1 slide scanner with each round of staining saved as a separate .CZI image file.

The following primary antibodies were used: αSMA (Dako, M0851; 1:500, 1 h at room temperature), β-catenin (Cell Marque, 224M-14; 1:500, 1.5 h at room temperature), E-cadherin (BD Biosciences, 610182; 1:200, 1 h at room temperature), CDX2 (Cell Signaling, 23083; 1:1,000, 1 h at room temperature), H3K9me2/3 (Cell Signaling, 5327; 1:200, 1 h at room temperature), pan-cytokeratin (Abcam, ab7753; 1:150, 1 h at room temperature), pan-cytokeratin (Invitrogen, MA5-13156; 1:100, 1 h at room temperature), PROX1 (Cell Signaling, 45546; 1:400, 1 h at room temperature), Ki-67 (Dako, M7240; 1:100, 1 h at room temperature), tenascin C (R&D Systems, MAB2138; 1:400, 1 h at room temperature), vimentin (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-6260; 1:400, 1 h at room temperature), ANXA1 (Abcam, ab214486; 1:500, overnight at 4 °C), YAP1 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-101199; 1:50, overnight at 4 °C) and a collagen-binding peptide (generated by the laboratory of V. Weaver61; 1:500, overnight at 4 °C). For pan-epithelial (pan-EPI) cocktail staining, the antibodies (Abcam, ab7753; Invitrogen, MA5-13156; and BD Biosciences, 610182) were combined, each at 1:200, and applied for 2 h at room temperature.

Immunofluorescence staining and imaging of TMAs was performed as previously described60 for pan-cadherin antibodies to label the tumour cells and their plasma membranes and the nuclear marker DAPI.

It has been revealed that preprocessing and segmentation were performed essentially as described previously36. In brief, TMA cores were de-arrayed using built-in tools from QuPath (v.0.5.1)62. Cores exhibiting folding artifacts, blurriness or limited tumour content were excluded from analysis. After preprocessing, nuclei were segmented based on DAPI signal using custom-trained Cellpose 2.0 models (v.2.0 and v.2.2.2)63, separately optimized for the TMA and whole-slide image datasets. The tumour and stromal compartments were identified using a multi-label U-Net trained on 30 representative cores. Pixel-level annotations were generated manually in ilastik (v.1.4.0)64 based on pan-EPI staining.

Tumour architectural subtypes were classified through a transfer-learning pipeline comprising four stages:.

Stage 1, tiling: each TMA core image was subdivided into non-overlapping 448 × 448 px (208 × 208 µm) tiles covering the full tissue area.

Stage 2, feature embedding: a multi-label U-Net was trained to segment architectural subtypes. Ground-truth masks were derived from the tumour–stroma segmentations described above, with tumour regions manually re-annotated according to three architectural subtypes: glandular (organized, lumen-forming structures), fragmented (disrupted tumour clusters) and solid (dense). Two additional classes (stroma and edge/background) were included to handle non-tumour regions. The training set comprised 196 cores selected as unambiguous archetypes of each architectural subtype. The validity of this selection was assessed by computing silhouette scores on a panel of interpretable morphological features (Fig. 1f) and comparing the archetype score to a null distribution generated from 1,000 size-matched random draws of cohort cores assigned matching per-class labels (Extended Data Fig. 2e). Each tile was then passed through the trained U-Net, and the activations at the deepest convolutional layer (bottleneck) were aggregated through global average pooling to yield a compact feature vector per tile, encoding the dominant morphological pattern without requiring a separate hand-crafted feature design.

Recent findings suggest that stage 3, tile-level classification: a multinomial logistic regression classifier (L-BFGS solver, scikit-learn) was trained on the bottleneck embeddings to assign each tile to one of five classes: glandular, fragmented, solid, stroma or edge/background. Features were standardized before classification. The training set comprised 1,154 manually annotated tiles (365 glandular, 251 fragmented, 148 solid, 199 stroma and 191 edge/background), randomly sampled from 760 cores across the cohort. Performance was evaluated using stratified fivefold cross-validation. At inference, the classifier output five class probabilities per tile; tiles dominated by edge or stroma (probability ≥ 0.5) were excluded, and the remaining glandular, fragmented and solid probabilities were renormalized to sum to one before assigning each tile to its most probable architectural subtype (argmax).

Stage 4, patient-level classification: tile-level predictions were aggregated per sample. The proportion of tumour-classified tiles belonging to each architectural subtype was computed separately for the CT (centre of the tumour) and IM. If a single subtype accounted for more than 50% of tiles, the sample was classified as that dominant architecture; otherwise, it was labelled mixed. The trained U-Net can be reused to extract morphological embeddings from other colorectal cancer datasets, provided that a membrane staining is available and that tissue tiles are of comparable physical size to those used in this study (448 × 448 pixels, corresponding to approximately 208 × 208 µm at the imaging resolution used here); tiles acquired at a different pixel resolution can be resampled (downsampled or upsampled) to match the model’s input size. However, the tile-level logistic regression classifier generally requires retraining to account for dataset-specific differences such as staining variability, imaging conditions or cohort composition. This is the strategy that we followed when applying the pipeline to the validation and multiplex datasets in this study: the U-Net embeddings were extracted directly, while the classifier was retrained on a new set of annotated tiles for each dataset. For the validation dataset, the classifier was retrained by supplementing the original training set with 205 additional annotated tiles (44 glandular, 49 fragmented, 28 solid, 50 stroma and 34 edge/background). For the multiplex dataset, 1,886 tiles were independently annotated (740 glandular, 446 fragmented, 123 solid, 491 stroma and 86 edge/background) and used to train a separate classifier. The pretrained U-Net model is available in ONNX format at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20343193).

It has been revealed that branch lengths were quantified from the binary tumour mask by first removing small objects (<20 px) and filling small holes (<100 px area), then skeletonizing the mask using skimage.morphology.skeletonize. Small spurious branches with an arc length of shorter than 5 pixels were removed by pruning using the skan library. Branch lengths were measured as geodesic arc lengths along the skeleton paths (√2-weighted pixel distances) using skan.summarize()[‘branch-distance’].

Industry observers note that the global contour roughness of the tumour boundary was assessed by extracting all contours from the binary tumour mask at level 0.5 using skimage.measure.find_contours. Contours with fewer than five points were discarded. The remaining contours were smoothed with a Gaussian filter (σ = 1) to reduce pixel noise. Pointwise curvature κ for a smoothed contour (x(s), y(s)) was computed by finite differences:.

It has been revealed that where primes denote derivatives with respect to the contour parameter. Absolute curvature values were summed over all contours and normalized by the total number of contour points N to yield mean roughness per unit length.

Recent findings suggest that lumens within the binary tumour mask were detected by filling all holes (scipy.ndimage.binary_fill_holes) and subtracting the original mask. The resulting lumen mask was labelled, and each lumen area (in pixels) was measured through skimage.measure.regionprops.

For each cell centroid, the Euclidean distances to its k = 3 nearest neighbours were computed using sklearn.neighbors.NearestNeighbors with a BallTree algorithm. For each cell, the mean, s.d., coefficient of variation and maximum of the k neighbour distances were stored as features.

According to recent reports, the local nuclear orientation order (Ψk) was computed for each cell using its k = 3 nearest neighbours. For each neighbour, the orientation angle θ was obtained by projecting the cell’s orientation vector (defined by its longest axis) onto a fixed reference direction. The nematic order parameter was then calculated as:.

yielding a value between 0 (random orientations) and 1 (perfectly aligned neighbours).

Stroma proximity was determined by computing, for each tumour cell centroid, the minimum Euclidean distance to the set of stroma cell centroids using pairwise distance computation (scipy.spatial.distance.cdist).

Tumour–stroma ratio was calculated by measuring the total pixel areas of the tumour and stroma compartments from the segmentation mask and computing the ratio of tumour pixel count to stroma pixel count.

Industry observers note that the fragmentation index was computed by first constructing a spatial proximity graph of all tumour cell centroids, where an edge connects any two cells of which the Euclidean distance is within 80 pixels (radius-based connectivity using a BallTree). Louvain community detection was then applied to this unweighted graph to partition cells into spatially coherent communities. The fragmentation index was calculated as the number of detected communities divided by the cell count.

Whole-core fluorescence images were segmented into 12 tissue compartments with a multi-scale tumour/stroma classifier, and tumour islands were defined as connected components of the tumour class on the cleaned compartment map after upsampling to image resolution. The stromal compartment was restricted to a strict definition that excluded muscle, vessel, adipose, dense-stroma and debris classes. For each tumour island, a peri-tumoural region of interest was constructed as the 50 µm band immediately outside the island border, intersected with the strict stroma mask. Within this region, fibre body masks were obtained for the collagen I and TNC channels (analysed independently) using a fine-tuned U-Net applied at a probability threshold of 0.5.

From each body mask, we derived three independent descriptors of the underlying fibre network65: (1) the box-counting fractal dimension of the binarized mask, capturing network roughness and branching complexity; (2) the mean structure-tensor coherence within the mask, ranging from 0 for isotropic networks to 1 for perfectly aligned fibres; and (3) the median local fibre thickness, computed as twice the Euclidean distance transform sampled along the fibre skeleton and converted to micrometres using a pixel size of 0.325 µm. Features were emitted per (image × island × channel × distance band × stroma definition × architecture) so that all downstream summaries remained traceable to the underlying islands and fluorescence pixels. To avoid within-image pseudoreplication, every subsequent comparison was performed on per-(image × architecture) means, obtained by averaging each feature across the islands sharing the same architecture within an image.

Whole-slide image immunostainings were registered using the warpy workflow in ImageJ and QuPath. Whole-slide images were subsequently divided into non-overlapping tiles of 1,000 × 1,000 pixels and selected for downstream analysis in a manner analogous to TMAs, including tumour/stroma classification and nuclear segmentation. For each nucleus, the average nuclear intensity of markers (ANXA1, SNAIL1) was quantified. For cytoplasmic markers (E-cadherin, ANXA1, VIM), the nuclear contour was dilated by 5 pixels to approximate the cytoplasmic region, from which the average cytoplasmic intensity was computed. Single-cell profiles were then clustered using the Leiden algorithm at a resolution of 0.1.

For each whole-slide-image tile, we computed a spatial-coherence score that quantifies whether cells with the same label group together or segregate. First, for every cell we counted its 12 immediate closest neighbours that shared the same label and averaged this count across all cells in the tile. Next, we generated a null range by randomly shuffling the position of all cells 100 times, repeating the same neighbour counting for each shuffle; the average value from these shuffled sets was taken as the expected mean. The score was then calculated as (observed – expected_mean)/(expected_max – expected_mean). A score above zero means cells with the same label cluster together more than would be expected by chance (attraction), a value of zero corresponds to a random arrangement and a negative value denotes spatial repulsion, where same-label cells are less likely to be adjacent than expected by chance.

In a recent development, TMA cores were identified using the dearrayer functionality in QuPath. Background illumination correction and background subtraction were subsequently performed for each core and staining round using PyBaSiC. TMAs were registered across six staining rounds using the DAPI channel as a reference. All cores underwent semi-manual quality control to remove samples that were damaged, exhibited poor registration or contained absent/very low tumour content.

Sources indicate that nuclear segmentation was performed using the Cellpose cyto3 model with the DAPI channel as the input. Tissue pixels were classified into tumour, stroma, tissue fold, autofluorescence, necrosis and background using an iterative supervised approach in ilastik until good visual agreement between pan-EPI signal and tumour masks was achieved across cores. For each cell, mean marker intensities were extracted using pyradiomics, and nuclear shape features were computed using a custom Python pipeline. To approximate cytoplasmic signal, nuclear masks were expanded by three pixels using expand_labels from skimage. We also computed, for each nucleus, the mean value of the ilastik pixel-classification probability map to derive cell-level classification confidence metrics.

Recent findings suggest that before clustering, cells with extreme nuclear areas were removed by excluding the lowest 1st percentile and highest 99th percentile. Tumour cells were then selected based on a tumour probability threshold of >0.5 and processed using a standard Scanpy workflow. Data were scaled using scanpy.pp.scale with max_value = 10, such that values were truncated to a maximum of 10 after scaling. Principal component analysis was performed using the maximum available number of components, and a k-nearest-neighbour graph was constructed with n_neighbors = 50. Clustering was performed using the Leiden algorithm with the igraph-based implementation.

For patient-level grouping, normalized phenotype distributions were used as input for hierarchical clustering (Ward linkage). The number of patient groups was determined based on biological interpretability and stability of the resulting clusters.

Tile-level U-Net embeddings were z-scored and used to build a k-nearest-neighbour graph, visualized by t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding (t-SNE). Partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) was computed on the three architecture classes (glandular, fragmented, solid, assigned by argmax of the renormalized U-Net probabilities after removing edge and stroma tiles) and overlaid on the t-SNE. Diffusion pseudotime was computed from a diffusion map of the same embeddings, rooted at the most confident glandular tile, and tiles were grouped into 40 equal-width pseudotime bins. Within each bin, architecture probabilities were averaged, and cell phenotype fractions (cells assigned to tiles by centroid position) were averaged and renormalized to unit sum.

Recent findings suggest that spatial transcriptomics was performed using the GeoMX-DSP platform (Nanostring/Bruker). Eight patients with stage II/III CRC were selected from the TMA cohort based on presence of architecturally heterogeneous tumours. Samples were prepared according to recommendations from the vendor for FFPE slides, including baking for 60 min at 60 °C, dewaxing and antigen retrieval with ER2 for 20 min at 100 °C, fixation in NBF (10%), incubation in NBF stop and proteinase K treatment (15 min at 37 °C). These steps were performed on the Leica BondRX autostainer. The slides were incubated with the probes overnight and, after stringent washes, were stained with Syto13, pan-cytokeratin (AF532), αSMA (custom conjugated on AF647) and CD45 (AF594) antibodies to detect tumour and stromal microenvironments. ROIs (67, 61, 96 and 59 for the four slides, carrying patients 1 and 2, 3 and 5, 4 and 6, and 7 and 8, respectively) were segmented for pan-cytokeratin positivity to collect 82, 94, 141 and 63 areas of interest (AOIs) representing tumour and tumour–stroma boundary. Each ROI yielded a tumour AOI and, where collected, a stroma AOI. Transcriptomic analyses of the tumour compartment (Figs. 2f, 4a,b and Extended Data Fig. 10a) used the 249 tumour AOIs from 8 patients. After scanning, tissue sections were additionally stained with antibodies against SNAIL1 (Santa Cruz, sc-271977), E-cadherin (BD, 610182), ANXA1 (Abcam, ab214486) and VIM (Santa Cruz, sc-6260) and imaged using Phenoimager (Akoya Biosciences).

Quality control of the sequencing data was performed in R using GeoMx packages, following standard GeoMx QC guidelines. Segment filtering employed the following thresholds: minimum reads per segment (AOI) = 1,000, minimum percentage of reads trimmed = 80, minimum percentage of reads stitched = 80, minimum percentage of reads aligned = 75, minimum sequencing saturation = 50, minimum negative control counts = 1, maximum counts in the NTC (no-template control) well = 9,000.

Segments with low signal were removed based on the limit of quantification. Gene filtering was applied by both compartment (tumour/stroma) and architecture type to preserve notable genes in underrepresented regions. A 10% segment cut-off was used. Data were normalized using the third quartile (Q3) method.

For differential gene expression, raw counts were analysed using the PyDESeq2 Python package, with patient sample included as a covariate to control for interpatient variability. For each gene, a Wald test was used to assess differential expression; multiple-testing correction was performed using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to control the FDR. Genes with an adjusted P value (q value) below 0.05 were considered significantly differentially expressed.

Sources indicate that gene set enrichment analysis was performed using the prerank function from the GSEApy Python package with 1,000 permutations. Before analysis, all genes were ranked according to their effect sizes (log-transformed fold changes) derived from the differential expression analysis. The following gene sets from previous studies were included. EMT gene sets: Wound response GO GP66, mesenchymal67, matrix remodelling68, TGFB activation (TGFB KEGG, TGFB CORE GENES/TGFB1/TGFB2)68,69, EMT activation (EMT Core Genes)67, EMT Hallmark70, pEMT71, EMT-II (MP13)72. SC gene sets: crypt base32, LGR5 intestinal SCs33, fetal8, regenerative34 and revival colonic SCs52. High-relapse gene sets: epithelial-specific high-risk gene set, core high-relapse cells73.

Industry observers note that trajectory analysis was performed using PAGA74 with the sc.tl.paga function built into Scanpy (v.1.9.6)75. To prepare the data, we first selected 3,000 highly variable genes using the seurat flavour of sc.pp.highly_variable_genes. Next, we calculated and selected 100 principal components (PCs) using sc.tl.pca. PCs were batch-corrected using Harmony (v.0.0.9)76 to correct for patient-specific gene expression profiles. Finally, nearest neighbours were calculated using sc.pp.neighbors (n_neighbors = 30) on the corrected PCs and PAGA was run on tumour architecture types.

We calculated diffusion pseudotime (DPT77) using the sc.tl.diffmap and sc.tl.dpt functions from Scanpy (v.1.9.6)75. In preparation, for a patient sample, we selected 3,000 highly variable genes using the seurat flavour of sc.pp.highly_variable_genes. Next, we calculated 100 principal components (PCs) using sc.tl.pca. Finally, nearest neighbours were calculated using sc.pp.neighbors (n_neighbors = 30) on the corrected PCs. DPT was run using a cell in the glandular region of the tumour as a ‘root cell’, representing its most unperturbed region.

The use of human CRC organoid cultures was approved as part of the iCAN Precision Medicine Flagship study reviewed by the HUS Ethical Committee and is executed based on a HUS research permit (4.5.2023 §38 (HUS/223/2023)), a Findata data permit (THL/1338/14.02.00/2022) and material transfer agreements with Helsinki Biobank (HBP20210170) and Finnish Hematology and Registry Biobank FHRB (12.5.2022). The underlying PANORG study collecting the samples to the iCAN Flagship was approved by the ethical committee of the Helsinki and Uusimaa hospital district and study site institutional review boards (PANORG ethical approval HUS/390/2021, HUS approval HUS/69/2022). The study participants provided written, informed consent for the protocols. Organoids were maintained in a mixture of 60% LWRN medium (originally established in ref. 78) and 40% human basal medium supplemented with rhEGF (R&D, 236-EG, 100 ng ml−1); LWRN was replaced with Advanced DMEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for no-WNT conditions. Organoids were subjected to single-cell sequencing and selected to harbour APC and TP53 mutations for the studies here.

Patient-derived CRC organoids were cultured in Matrigel or collagen (drug treatment experiment), after which single-cell suspensions were generated by incubation with cell recovery solution (30 min at 4 °C; Corning) followed by digestion with TrypLE Express Enzyme (5 min at 37 °C; Invitrogen). After washing with ice-cold DMEM, single cells were counted using Luna-II automated cell counter (Logos Biosystems) and loaded on a microwell cartridge of the BD Rhapsody Express system (BD) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Single-cell whole-transcriptome analysis libraries were prepared according to the manufacturer’s instructions using the BD Rhapsody WTA Reagent kit (BD, 633802) and sequenced on the Illumina NextSeq 500 system using the High Output Kit v2.5 (150 cycles, Illumina) for 2 × 75 bp paired-end reads with 8 bp single index aiming sequencing depth of >20,000 reads per cell for each sample.

Recent findings suggest that UMI, complex barcode, and sample tags were extracted from raw reads and demultiplexed using a custom script (rhapsody-demultiplex; https://github.com/Bioinformatics-Service-MPI-Munster/scrna-tools). Reads were mapped using STAR (v.2.7.10a)79 (--soloType CB_UMI_Complex --soloCellFilter None --outSAMtype BAM SortedByCoordinate --soloFeatures GeneFull_Ex50pAS --soloAdapterSequence NNNNNNNNNGTGANNNNNNNNNGACA --soloCBmatchWLtype 1MM --soloCBposition 2_0_2_8 2_13_2_21 3_1_3_9 --soloUMIposition 3_10_3_17 --soloCBwhitelist BD_CLS1_v2_draft.txt BD_CLS2_v2_draft.txt BD_CLS3_v2_draft.txt --runRNGseed 1 --soloMultiMappers EM --readFilesCommand zcat --outSAMattributes NH HI AS nM NM MD jM jI MC ch CB UB GX GN). Raw counts were imported as AnnData (v.0.10.7)80 objects in Python (v.3.9.11). We removed low-complexity barcodes using the knee plot method (1,500–3,000 counts per cell) and further filtered out cells with a high mitochondrial mRNA percentage (>50%). Doublets were predicted with scrublet (v.0.2.3)81. Finally, each sample’s gene expression matrix was normalized using scran (v.1.26.2)82, with Leiden clustering83 input at resolution 0.5.

At this stage, the samples were merged with scanpy (v.1.10.1)75. For 2D embedding, expression values were cell cycle regressed using sc.tl.score_genes_cell_cycle with G2M and S-phase gene lists from ref. 84 and sc.pp.regress_out. The expression matrix was subset to the 3,000 most highly variable genes (sc.pp.highly_variable_genes, flavor=“seurat”). We calculated and selected the top 100 PCs (sc.tl.pca), which served as basis for k-nearest neighbour calculation (sc.pp.neighbors, n_neighbors = 30). Nearest neighbours were then used as an input for UMAP layout (sc.tl.umap, min_dist = 0.3). Leiden clusters were calculated using sc.tl.leiden at resolution 0.7. Pseudotime and gene set enrichment analyses were performed as described for the spatial transcriptomics datasets. For reanalysis of the published tumour in vivo data, we chose a cell in the most stem-like cluster according to CytoTRACE analysis.

For generation of consensus gene sets, EMT gene sets (mesenchymal67, matrix remodelling68, TGFB activation (TGFB KEGG, TGFB CORE GENES/TGFB1/TGFB2)68,69, EMT activation (EMT Core Genes67, EMT Hallmark70, pEMT71, EMT-II (MP13)72) and SC gene sets (crypt base32, LGR5 intestinal SCs33, fetal8, regenerative34 and revival colonic SCs52) were merged and overlapping genes within and across gene sets were removed to generate the Core-EMT, Core-CBC and Core-RegSC gene sets.

Sources indicate that all cells in the dataset were scored for the Core-EMT, Core-CBC and Core-RegSC gene sets using the Scanpy sc.tl.score_genes function. The scores were then converted to a per-dataset rank rescaled to [0, 1]. Cells were then ordered across the CBC to RegSC–EMT axis as a composite_trajectory = (RegSC_rank01 + EMT_rank01 − CBC_rank01 + 1)/3. Cells with composite_trajectory in the top 30% of the per-dataset distribution were classified hybrid.

For distribution across the EMT–RegSC axis, two curated marker panels were scored per hybrid cell with sc.tl.score_genes (random_state = 0): a RegSC-pole panel (GPRC5A, TSPAN1, PDZK1IP1, ANXA1, ANXA3, S100A6, S100A11, LCN2, SAA1, SAA2, KRT16, KRT17, SPP1, CD44, EMP1 and TACSTD2) and an EMT pole panel (SNAI1, SNAI2, ZEB1, ZEB2, TWIST1, TWIST2, VIM, FN1, S100A4, ACTA2, MMP14, PLAU, PLAUR, SERPINE1, TIMP1). Each panel score was z-scored within its dataset, and the pole axis was defined as axis_pole = z(score_EMT_pole) − z(score_RegSC_pole). The pole-axis shift among hybrid cells was computed as Cliff’s δ = 2 × U/(n_c × n_Unt) − 1, where U is the Mann–Whitney U statistic of axis pole over the two hybrid groups. δ ∈ [−1, +1]; δ < 0 represents that hybrid cells of c are shifted toward the regenerative pole relative to untreated-hybrid cells, δ > 0 represents that hybrid cells of c are shifted toward the EMT pole. By default, untreated sits at δ = 0.

Recent findings suggest that hydrogel scaffolds were engineered as described previously42,85. A PDMS stamp (see below) with a crypt-mimicking array of pillar topography was placed in the central top reservoir of the chip. To generate the ECM for the chip, bovine TeloCol-6 type I collagen solution (5225-50mL, Advanced Biomatrix) was neutralized according to the manufacturer’s instructions and then mixed with Matrigel (356231, Corning) at a 75/25 (v/v) ratio. After gel injection through gel-loading port, hydrogel was polymerized at 37 °C, 5% CO2 (hereafter referred to as incubator) for 15 min. After ECM polymerization, all chip reservoirs were topped up with PBS or cell culture medium.

Recent findings suggest that stamps featuring crypt-mimicking microtopography were fabricated from PDMS by replica moulding of 2PP-printed models. First, arrays of colon crypt-mimicking micropillars were designed in Autodesk Fusion. Several topographies were tested and optimized, the final microtopography design consists of the slightly conical pillars, ranging from 50 to 120 µm in diameter (top to bottom) and 700 µm in height. The 3D model was printed using a NanoOne (UpNano) 2PP printer on glass coverslips with UpPhoto resin and a ×10/0.4 NA objective. To generate a master mould with inverted topography, the printed structures were plasma-activated and silanized overnight using vapour-phase trichloro(1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyl) silane (Sigma-Aldrich). PDMS (Sylgard 184, Dow Corning; 10:1 base-to-curing agent ratio) was poured over the master, degassed under vacuum, and cured at 80 °C for 12 h. The resulting PDMS replica was cut, plasma-activated and silanized overnight as above. This PDMS negative was then used repeatedly as a mould for casting final PDMS stamps using the same procedure (Sylgard 184, 10:1 ratio, cured at 80 °C for 12 h).

Organoids were dissociated using TrypLE Express (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and resuspended at 40 million cells per ml in Advanced DMEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 10 µM Y27632 after which 5 µl of cell suspension was plated onto each chip. Cells were allowed to settle for 1 h in a cell culture incubator, after which the chips were filled with Y27632-supplemented medium. The next day, Y27632 was removed and cells were cultured for 5 days. Chips were fixed in 4% PFA for 16 h at 4 °C, placed into 3D-printed custom histomoulds, filled with HistoGel (Thermo Fisher Scientific), embedded in paraffin and sectioned as described previously86. The samples were then processed for RNA in situ hybridization or immunofluorescence as described below.

It has been revealed that in situ hybridization was performed using RNAscope technology (Advanced Cell Diagnostics) according to the manufacturer’s protocols. In brief, organoids were fixed in 4% PFA for 30 min at 37 °C, rinsed with PBS, dehydrated in a graded ethanol series and air dried. The slides were then rehydrated and 2 drops of hydrogen peroxide were added to each slide for 10 min. Primary antibodies were added and incubated overnight at 4 °C. The slides were washed and fixed with 4% PFA for 30 min at room temperature. After PBS washes, three drops of 1:15 diluted Protease Plus were added to slides and incubated for 10 min, followed by PBS washes.

Recent findings suggest that RNA probes were prewarmed for 10 min at 40 °C, cooled down and added onto slides. The slides were incubated with probes for 2 h at 40 °C, washed twice with wash buffer, subjected to stepwise hybridization with amplifier solutions for 15 min each at 40 °C, followed by application of blocker solutions. Finally, samples were incubated with Alexa-conjugated secondary antibodies diluted in co-detection antibody diluent for 30 min at room temperature. After washes and brief incubation with DAPI, the slides were mounted in Elvanol and imaged. The following probes were used: ANXA1-c3 465411, LGR5-c2 311021, OLFM4-c1 311041, VIM-c1 310441. Images were obtained using the Zeiss LSM980 system using ×20 air and ×40 water objectives. Channels were acquired sequentially at room temperature using Zeiss Zen Blue software (v.3.13).

Organoids were fixed in 4% PFA for 1 h at room temperature, permeabilized in 0.6% Triton X-100 for 30 min, blocked with 5% BSA and 5% goat serum in PBS for 2 h, after which primary antibodies were added in blocking solution and incubated overnight at 4 °C. After multiple washes in PBS, secondary Alexa Fluor-conjugated antibodies were added in 1% BSA, 1% goat serum for 2 h at room temperature. Organoids were then mounted in ProLong Gold (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The following primary antibodies were used: ANXA1 (Abcam, ab214486, 1:1,000, overnight, 4 °C), YAP1 (Santa Cruz, sc-101199, 1:500, overnight, 4 °C), active YAP (Abcam, ab205270, 1:100, overnight, 4 °C), β-catenin (Cell Marque, 224M-14, 1:100, overnight, 4 °C), SNAIL1 (Santa Cruz, sc-271977, 1:50, overnight, 4 °C), HP1α (Cell Signaling, 2616, 1:200, overnight, 4 °C), lamin A/C (Cell Signaling, 2032, 1:200, overnight, 4 °C), SOX4 (Abcam, ab236557, 1:400, overnight, 4 °C), pSMAD2/3 (Cell Signaling, 3108, 1:100, overnight, 4 °C). Images were obtained using either the Zeiss LSM980 or Nikon Yokogawa CSU-W1 system with ×20 air and ×40 water objectives. Channels were acquired sequentially at room temperature using Zeiss Zen Blue software (v.3.13) or NIS Elements (AR 5.41.01).

To mechanically compress the organoids, organoids grown in Matrigel for 5 days were replated on top of Matrigel-coated 12–20 mm round glass coverslips and allowed to attach for 24 h. After attachment, the organoids were sandwiched with another 12–20 mm coverslip with a weight applying 200 Pa of vertical stress (generating a 45% reduction in organoid height) for 20 h.

It has been revealed that for 3D organoid imaging, single cells were first embedded in 8 mg ml−1 Matrigel and, after 4 days of culture, were transferred either to fresh Matrigel or pH-adjusted 1 mg ml−1 collagen I matrices. The organoids were treated with 5 µM TDI-011536 (MedChemExpress, HY-150042), 10 ng ml−1 TGFβ1 (StemCell Technologies, 78067.1) or both with daily medium replenishment while being live-cell imaged every 30 min with a Sartorius Incucyte S3 incubator microscope for up to 4 days.

Bright-field images were segmented using Cellpose4-SAM87 and edge detection followed by morphological gap-closing and hole-filling to obtain binary organoid masks that were imported to ImageJ (Fiji). MorphoLibJ88 was used to quantify convexity, Geodesic diameter, Geodesic elongation and organoid area that were scaled between 0 and 1 to initially classify the organoids into expanded, dispersive or cohesive classes in an unbiased manner. As the resolution of the masks was not sufficient to accurately capture surface structures, the classifications were all manually inspected further and assigned to the final classes.

RNA was isolated using the NucleoSpin RNA plus Kit (Macherey-Nagel). RNA quality was assessed using the high-sensitivity RNA Screen Tape Analysis (TapeStation, Agilent) and subsequently 500 ng of RNA was reverse transcribed applying the SuperScript IV VILO Master Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. PCR was performed using the PowerUp SYBR Green Mastermix (Thermo Fisher Scientific) on the QuantStudio5 Real-Time PCR System (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Gene expression was quantified using the ΔΔCt method with normalization to B2M. The following primers were used. B2M: forward primer, GAGTATGCCTGCCGTGTGAA; reverse primer, GCTTACATGTCTCGATCCCACT; AXIN2: forward primer, GCGCTGACGGATGATTCCAT; reverse primer, TGGGTTCTCGGGAAATGAGGT; ASCL2: forward primer, CGCCTACTCGTCGGACGACAG; reverse primer, GCCGCTCGCTCGGCTTCCG.

Mouse colonoscopy was performed using the TELE PACK+VET system (Karl Storz, RP101S1). Illumination was provided by a xenon light source connected through the Adapt. KST fibre-optic light cable/Xenon 100 (495KS). The system includes a camera control, air insufflation units and an integrated endoscopic video unit with built-in documentation and memory storage. Colonoscopy imaging was performed using an integrated multipurpose Hopkins Telescope (67031BA) with an outer diameter of 11.5 Fr. Images were acquired using an IMAGE1 S HX FULL HD Camera Head (TH110). Mice were anaesthetized with isoflurane and organoid fragments corresponding to 5 × 105 single cells were transplanted into the colonic submucosa using a Hamilton syringe (Hamilton, Reno, 7656-01) equipped with a transfer needle for sample loading (7770-02) and an injection needle (7803-05). The needle was carefully inserted into the colonic submucosa, and 50 µl of organoid fragments suspended in 1 mg ml−1 rat collagen type 1 (Sigma-Aldrich, C3867) supplemented with 10% Corning Matrigel (Corning, 356231) was delivered and generated a visible submucosal bleb. The mice were treated for 5 days after transplantation with the LATS kinase inhibitor TDI-011536 (MedChemExpress, HY-150042). TDI-011536 was prepared at a concentration of 5 mg ml−1 by emulsification in 10% Kolliphor HS 15 (Merck, 42966) in PBS and administered by oral gavage twice daily at a dose of 2.5 mg per kg. Vehicle-treated animals received 10% Kolliphor in PBS alone.

It has been revealed that TGFβ1 treatment was performed using human recombinant TGFβ1 (StemCell Technologies, 78067.1) within Affi-Gel Blue beads (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 153-7301). In brief, beads were washed four times with ice-cold bi-distilled water and incubated overnight with 500 µl of 50 µg ml−1 TGFβ1 in PBS supplemented with 10 mM HEPES. TGFβ1-loaded beads were mixed with organoid fragments in collagen solution at a final proportion of 10% (v/v) before implantation. For dual-treatment experiments, animals received both TDI-011536 administration and TGFβ1-loaded beads as described above. Each treatment group consisted of four mice (n = 4). Mice were monitored three times per week, and colonoscopy imaging was performed every 2 weeks for 4 weeks before euthanasia.

Industry observers note that tissue biopsies (intestinal rolls) were fixed in 4% PFA, embedded in paraffin and sectioned. Sections were de-paraffinized using a graded alcohol series and antigen retrieval was carried out using target retrieval solution (Dako) at pH 6 or pH 9 in a pressure cooker. Unspecific binding was blocked using 5% normal goat serum, 3% BSA in PBS, after which antibodies were diluted in DAKO antibody diluent and incubated overnight in a moist chamber at 4 °C. After PBS washes, Alexa-Fluor-conjugated secondary antibodies were diluted in 1% BSA in PBS, incubated for 1 h at room temperature, after which samples were mounted in Elvanol. The following primary antibodies were used: ANXA1 (Abcam, ab214486), pSMAD2/3 (Cell Signaling, 3108) and active YAP (Abcam ab205270). Images were obtained using the Zeiss LSM980 system with ×20 air and ×40 water objectives. Channels were acquired sequentially at room temperature using Zeiss Zen Blue software (v.3.13). The tumour area was quantified using ANXA1 staining to generate a ROI mask in Fiji. The number of ROIs was used to extract the lesion number.

It has been revealed that all animal experiments were performed in accordance with EU Directive 2010/63/EU and Finnish legislation, and were approved by the National Animal Experiment Board of Finland (ELLA) under project licence ESAVI/30305/2023. Female NOD.Cg-PrkdcscidIl2rgtm1Wjl/SzJ (NSG) mice (The Jackson Laboratory, 005557) were used at 12 weeks of age at the start of the experiment. Sample size was determined using the resource equation method (E = N − T), where N is the total number of animals and T the number of groups; with four groups of four mice (N = 16), E = 12, within the recommended range of 10–20. Mice were randomly allocated to experimental groups; no formal randomization method was used. Tumour implantation was confirmed in all mice, and animals were euthanized and dissected 4 weeks after transplantation. No mice reached the humane end-point limits defined in the licence, and no mice were excluded from the analysis.

Sources indicate that statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software (GraphPad, v.9) or in R (v.2023.09.1+494). Statistical significance was determined using the specific tests indicated in the corresponding figure legends. Only two-tailed tests were used. In all cases in which a test for normally distributed data was used, normal distribution was confirmed using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test (α = 0.05). All experiments presented in the manuscript were repeated at least in three independent replicates. Automated software algorithms were used for unbiased quantification of staining intensities, sequencing data and architecture features/cell shapes in all experiments involving these techniques so blinding was not relevant. For animal experiments endoscopy and sample collection were performed in a blinded manner. For manual organoid invasion pattern classification blinding was applied during data analysis. No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes. Sample size was determined based on previous experience, published literature, or to specific requirements of a given technique.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

The single-cell sequencing data are available at the GEO (GSE297054 and GSE333618). Spatial transcriptomics data have been uploaded to Keeper (https://keeper.mpdl.mpg.de/d/4033948ddc0b4e06aaeb/). All patient-related data (TMA and spatial transcriptomics post-hoc staining) have been deposited in the Helsinki Biobank (HBP20210170) and Finnish Hematology and Registry Biobank FHRB (12.5.2022). The pretrained U-Net model is available in ONNX format at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20343193)89. All in vitro data are available from the authors on request. Source data are provided with this paper.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable companies, grapples with CEO Jensen Huang's romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, attention is turning to the much smaller organization she worked for.

It has been revealed that alice H., the alleged spy, worked as an executive for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center and AI computing company. It manages data center access, including for some major Chinese tech firms such as Alibaba.

According to Megaspeed's website as of November 2026, the manufacturer advertises itself as an "Nvidia cloud partner", saying it provides "computing power product services covering Nvidia's entire GPU product line." GPU stands for Graphic Processing Unit, a specialized electronic circuit that are in high demand for artificial intelligence (AI) applications, because they are designed to handle high numbers of parallel mathematical calculations. Megaspeed claims it provides access for clients to Nvidia's advanced GB200 NVL72 ​computing system.

This type of firm is often referred to as a "neocloud". It buys Nvidia chips and computing power and then rents it out — in this case, at multiple sites across south-east Asia, to different companies. The US has set up strict export controls to prevent that Nvidia's high-performance chips end up in China, because it sees China as a competitor in the global AI race. It also does not want data centers made up of Nvidia chips to be owned by Chinese companies. It does, however, tolerate that data center compute with Nvidia chips be rented out to Chinese companies like Alibaba, and occasionally allows the export of Nvidia chips for specific purposes.

Megaspeed has bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia's products in recent years and has been accused of breaching US export controls to divert Nvidia chips into China.

In December 2025, Bloomberg reported that the "once-obscure" Megaspeed had become the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in all of south-east Asia and that the US government was investigating its ownership structure and whether or not it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China.

At the same time, Singapore police began an investigation into whether or not Megaspeed had "violated local laws" without specifying which ones. Those investigations are believed to be still ongoing.

On December 23, 2025, Megaspeed strenuously denied any wrongdoing in a statement — which still appears as the first page for visitors to the manufacturer's website as of November 2026.

Industry observers note that "There has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate firm," it noted. "We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct.".

In a recent development, the US government investigation began in 2024. The Commerce Department initially began looking into Megaspeed, but the US Justice Department has since taken over. According to the Upcoming York Times, this switch came about after an Nvidia executive directly contacted the Commerce Department about the investigation.

Sources indicate that megaspeed was founded in 2015 and was originally called 7Road International. It changed its name to Megaspeed in March 2023. It is owned by the Singapore-registered Swiftdata, which was set up in October 2023.

Its rise in prominence coincided with a sharp increase in assets, which increased from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024.

Alice H., the woman accused of being a Chinese spy, had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. She is widely seen as an influential figurehead at Megaspeed. She also served as the company's managing director of Megaspeed for eight months in 2023.

According to recent reports, the Financial Times reported on Monday that Alice H. leveraged her close access to Jensen Huang and Nvidia to pitch AI chips deals to Chinese investors.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The newspaper said that in early 2025, Alice H. sought investment in China for a data center project in south-east Asia, and cited their easy access to Nvidia chips and close relationship with Alibaba.

Recent findings suggest that alibaba lent money to Megaspeed in June 2024, via subsidiaries. It has remained Megaspeed's largest client, according to reporting by the Financial Times.

In December 2025, Nvidia said its own inquiry into Megaspeed had found no evidence of chips being diverted and that the company was fully owned and operated outside of China, with no Chinese shareholders. The company told Bloomberg at the time that it had visited Megaspeed's facilities on multiple occasions and had seen nothing untoward.

Megaspeed is one of several companies accused of smuggling Nvidia's chips into China or finding ways to give Chinese companies access to them.

Nvidia's high-performance chips are seen as essential for companies looking for the most advanced form of supercomputing to use and develop various AI applications.

Back in 2022, the Biden Administration began severely restricting the sale of the US's most advanced chips to China, part of the two countries' growing rivalry to achieve AI dominance.

However, an illegal smuggling and underground network was soon set up, with many vendors operating to get the chips into China and selling them on to companies there.

In December 2025, US authorities shut down the operations of Hao Global, a US-based shell company with links to China which plead guilty to smuggling Nvidia chips to China.

In June 2026, Taiwanese government agencies raided the offices of Super Micro Computer as part of an investigation into the smuggling of Nvidia chips to China.

While export restrictions have been eased significantly under the Trump administration, there are still significant blocks and restrictions on the most advanced Nvidia chips.

In December 2025, the Trump administration approved several Chinese companies to buy or handle advanced Nvidia H200 chips, a move that sparked significant concern among the US security establishment.

However, that deal has not led to a significant flow of Nvidia chips moving legally to China, amid strict US licencing controls and official reluctance from Beijing to publicly promote Nvidia chips to the detriment of its own alternatives.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hill Dickinson Stadium welcomed some of Liverpool’s care experienced young people for an exclusive behind-the-scenes tour to mark National Care Leavers Month. A group of 25 care leavers, who have either left or are preparing to leave local authority care, were given the opportunity to explore the Club’s stunning waterfront home. Observed every November, National Care Leavers Month is a UK-wide campaign that celebrates care experienced young people, amplifies their voices and promotes positive change in policy and practice. The youngsters, many of whom were visiting a football stadium for the first time, enjoyed an informative tour of the state-of-the-art venue, including the impressive home dressing room, the Media Centre, pitchside areas and learning about the heritage of the historic site. Jenny Glennard, Corporate Director of Children & Young People’s Services at Liverpool City Council, noted: "On behalf of Liverpool Children's Social Care, I would like to again extend my gratitude to Everton for providing our care experienced young people with the fantastic opportunity to visit Hill Dickinson Stadium as part of National Care Leavers Month. "To be given a personal group tour was an experience and memory they will never forget. All of our young people have expressed how much they enjoyed the day and how impressed they were with the stadium, as well as the staff who made them feel so welcome. "We value our relationship with Everton and look forward to continuing to work with the Club in the future." Liverpool City Council's Leaving Care Services provide a wide range of support for young people transitioning from local authority care. Using a person-centred approach to independent living skills, planning and assessment, the service aims to improve outcomes across education, training, employment, health and accommodation. For more information on Liverpool City Council's Leaving Care Services, click here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This Brighton and Hove Albion title challenge – as it must now be classed – flies in the face of the saying that money always talks in football. Manchester City have been found guilty of breaching financial rules and also fielded the most expensive midfield in Premier League history here, yet the match-winners cost a fraction in comparison.

Looking at Brighton’s winning goal, it was created by a cross that flashed across the City goal from Diego Gómez, an £11m signing who was playing in Major League Soccer in the United States not so long ago. Maxim de Cuyper, a £17.5m arrival from Club Brugge, was credited with the assist after Yasin Ayari tapped in.

Ayari cost £3.5m from Swedish club AIK and scored in the 5-0 wins over Coventry and Palace, and now has this winner to add to his collection. The 23-year-old is another example of Brighton polishing these gems and putting them together in a team that can win against any opponent in the Premier League.

According to recent reports, it could keep them at the top end of the table for a good while longer. They have already shown they can defeat Arsenal in a one-off match and they look to have the ingredients to stay the pace with them. In Fabian Hürzeler they have one of the brightest young coaches in the Premier League and he has a squad that are all on the same page.

Leicester upset the odds 10 years ago with a settled team, while this Brighton team has a deeper squad. When the substitutes came on in the second half, they slotted into a well-rehearsed system.

“We faced adversity. There was a little bit of luck but in the end they deserved it because they worked hard for it,” noted Hürzeler. “I want players who want to compete, to dominate. They all have the winning mentality inside of them. These kinds of performances are not about one or two players, everyone has to stick together.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Everton has announced a newly introduced multi-year partnership with global power technology brand NOCO. The agreement will see the US-headquartered company become Everton’s 'Official Battery Charging Partner', further strengthening the Club’s growing portfolio of international commercial partners. Founded in Cleveland, Ohio in 1914, NOCO has established itself as an internationally-recognised name in power technology, specialising in battery chargers, portable jump starters, tyre inflators, lithium batteries and related accessories. With more than 110 years of innovation behind it, the company has developed a significant international presence, with offices and operations spanning North America, Europe, Asia and Australia. As part of the partnership, NOCO will benefit from prominent brand visibility across Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium, with LED perimeter advertising and exposure through the Club’s digital and social media channels. The agreement will also provide NOCO with opportunities to host international clients and business guests and events at Everton fixtures at Hill Dickinson Stadium, using the Club’s matchday experiences to develop relationships and support its global business network. Mark Rollings, Chief Partnerships Officer at Everton, remarked: “We are delighted to welcome NOCO to Everton. “NOCO is a well-established and respected international business with a proud heritage, a strong reputation for innovation and clear ambitions for continued global growth. “Securing a brand of NOCO’s standing in a new commercial category is another positive step in the development of our partnership portfolio. It also demonstrates Everton’s growing profile and the opportunities we can offer international businesses looking to build their brand through the global reach of the Premier League. “NOCO joins an impressive group of globally recognised businesses already working with Everton, and we look forward to building a successful relationship that supports its continued growth.” The partnership comes at a time of continued international expansion for NOCO, which has strengthened its presence in key overseas markets, including a recent agreement with AUTOBACS Global, one of Japan’s leading automotive retailers. NOCO was also recently recognised at the 2026 Circana Automotive Aftermarket Performance Awards, winning the Maintenance & Repair category for achieving the highest increase in US market share. Zachary Koehler, Partnership Marketing Manager at NOCO, said: We’re proud to partner with Everton, a club with a rich history and one of the most passionate fanbases in world football. “Like Everton, NOCO is built on more than a century of heritage and a drive to keep moving forward. As we continue to grow internationally, the global reach of the Premier League gives us a powerful platform to connect with new audiences, customers, and partners. “We can’t think of a better way to make our debut than the Merseyside derby, and we look forward to a successful partnership with everyone at Everton."  The agreement will see NOCO branding formally make its debut at Everton’s next home fixture, the Merseyside derby, and further underlines the Club’s growing commercial momentum and international appeal. NOCO joins an expanding portfolio of globally recognised brands associated with Everton, including Pepsi, Budweiser, Castore, Red Bull, Heinz, Nestlé, JYSK and Christopher Ward.

Everton has announced a newly introduced multi-year partnership with global power technology brand NOCO.

The agreement will see the US-headquartered manufacturer become Everton’s 'Official Battery Charging Partner', further strengthening the Club’s growing portfolio of international commercial partners.

Founded in Cleveland, Ohio in 1914, NOCO has established itself as an internationally-recognised name in power technology, specialising in battery chargers, portable jump starters, tyre inflators, lithium batteries and related accessories.

With more than 110 years of innovation behind it, the company has developed a significant international presence, with offices and operations spanning North America, Europe, Asia and Australia.

As part of the partnership, NOCO will benefit from prominent brand visibility across Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium, with LED perimeter advertising and exposure through the Club’s digital and social media channels.

The agreement will also provide NOCO with opportunities to host international clients and business guests and events at Everton fixtures at Hill Dickinson Stadium, using the Club’s matchday experiences to develop relationships and support its global business network.

Mark Rollings, Chief Partnerships Officer at Everton, remarked: “We are delighted to welcome NOCO to Everton.

“NOCO is a well-established and respected international business with a proud heritage, a strong reputation for innovation and clear ambitions for continued global growth.

“Securing a brand of NOCO’s standing in a new commercial category is another positive step in the development of our partnership portfolio. It also demonstrates Everton’s growing profile and the opportunities we can offer international businesses looking to build their brand through the global reach of the Premier League.

“NOCO joins an impressive group of globally recognised businesses already working with Everton, and we look forward to building a successful relationship that supports its continued growth.”.

The partnership comes at a time of continued international expansion for NOCO, which has strengthened its presence in key overseas markets, including a recent agreement with AUTOBACS Global, one of Japan’s leading automotive retailers.

NOCO was also recently recognised at the 2026 Circana Automotive Aftermarket Performance Awards, winning the Maintenance & Repair category for achieving the highest increase in US market share.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 17:18 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 05:01 EST, 26 November 2026.
  • A week into the job and Mauricio Pochettino must be getting used to the madness of Manchester United by now.
  • If it's not drones flying over the training ground, red card controversies and random divots of grass, it's his own players shooting themselves in the foot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 17:18 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 05:01 EST, 26 November 2026.

A week into the job and Mauricio Pochettino must be getting used to the madness of Manchester United by now.

If it's not drones flying over the training ground, red card controversies and random divots of grass, it's his own players shooting themselves in the foot.

At least, Pochettino emerged from the craziness in Lisbon with a draw on a night when Bruno Fernandes celebrated his return to the Jose Alvalade Stadium with a couple of goals.

Industry observers note that but these are the kind of nights that must drive coaches like Pochettino potty. After the carnage of Michael Carrick's final two games in charge against Roma and Aston Villa, and the rancour of the Argentine's introduction to the Old Trafford circus at Anfield on Sunday, this was another mad, mad spectacle.

Where do we start? The two acts of self-sabotage by goalkeeper Senne Lammens? United's two disallowed goals? The first was harsh on the scorer, Amad Diallo, but also Youri Tielemans who received a booking that led to his sending-off in injury-time. Or maybe that divot, which Fernandes claimed he created and then hit to put United ahead with a bizarre deflected goal?

At the end of all the chaos, United had conceded five penalties in their last five games and picked up four red cards.

Senne Lammens (left) two errors cost Man United a deserving win at Sporting as they drew.

New United head coach Mauricio Pochettino comforts Lammens at full-time after his mistakes.

Recent findings suggest that that is not something that will sit well with Pochettino. But after venting his frustration with the officiating over Leny Yoro's sending-off at Anfield, which dominated the build-up to this game after it was rescinded, here was another sequence of events that seemed to conspire against him.

It's not as if the Jose Alvalade Stadium was a cauldron of emotion to scramble the senses of the two sets of players and match officials either. Fernandes got a polite round of applause from the fans and a framed memento from his old club before kick-off.

When the teams came out, he was one of three former United players alongside Cristiano Ronaldo and Luis Nani honoured on a tifo of the Sporting Lisbon greats.

Sources indicate that it was all very flat until the half-hour mark when United self-imploded again. Geny Catamo picked up the ball on the edge of the United box and teased Lisandro Martinez, playing at left back.

Industry observers note that martinez took the bait and stuck his leg out. He barely caught Sporting's No 10 and it took Catamo a full second to realise he had, before going down theatrically and earning a very soft penalty from Polish referee Szymon Marciniak.

Sporting's top scorer Luis Suarez stepped up and made it easy for Lammens to make the save. It was a let-off for United and potentially a big moment in a difficult season for Lammens.

But he undid his good work 75 seconds later when Maxi Araujo chased a long ball over the top pursued by Noussair Mazraoui. For some reason, Lammens thought it would be a good idea to race 25 yards out of his goal.

Araujo stepped inside the Belgium goalkeeper and went down under his clumsy challenge. Marciniak pointed to the spot again, and this time Suarez made no mistake.

Lammens started positively saving this Luis Suarez penalty before conceding a spot-kick.

Yet, minutes later Suarez scored after being given a second penalty following Lammens error.

United thought they had eqaulised before half-time but Amad Diallo's header was ruled out for a percieved foul in the build-up by Youri Tielemans that earned him a booking.

After all the upset over the officiating at Anfield, United were on the wrong end of another substantial call just before half-time here when Tielemans stretched to poke the ball through to Diallo and inadvertently caught Goncalo Inacio who went down claiming serious injury.

According to recent reports, goalkeeper Kaique Pereira saved Diallo's first effort and Marciniak blew his whistle for a foul before the Ivorian headed in at the second attempt so there was no opportunity for VAR to review it. The referee booked Tielemans, but there was a strong argument that it wasn't even a foul.

United re-emerged for the second half undeterred and hit back to score twice through Fernandes within five minutes of the restart.

The United captain played the ball through for Martinez and then converted from the spot after his team-mate went down in a tangle of legs with Eduardo Quaresma.

Bruno Fernandes levelled for United just after half-time when they were awarded a penalty.

He then put them ahead with this left-footed shot that hit a divot on the pitch before flying in.

United's lead was undone late on when Lammens' second major error allowed Suarez to score.

United's evening was compounded when Tielemans was sent off late on for a second yellow.

Two minutes later, and having made the divot turning in the penalty box 17 seconds earlier, Fernandes somehow managed to hit it with a hopeful effort from 25 yards. Pereira had the ball covered but it took an outrageous deflection just outside the six-yard box and flew through his arms.

In a recent development, but this is United and nothing is straightforward. In the 80th minute, with victory within their grasp, Lammens had all the time in the world to catch a high ball from Ivan Fresneda. Perhaps too long. Unforgivably, he dropped it in front of Suarez who hooked into the net.

There was still time for more drama when United had another goal from a Fernandes' corner chalked off for Patrick Dorgu's foul on Pereira, after VAR sent Marciniak to the monitor, and he then indicated Tielemans a second yellow card.

Pochettino looked on frustrated and probably as confused as the rest of us.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Unsurprisingly, Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is no exception.
  • Sources indicate that but when Klopp gave ter Stegen the nod, Urbig was still spending most of his time on the bench in Munich.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's no secret that getting playing time is vital to the development of any professional footballer – especially if your aspiration is to become the first-choice goalkeeper for your country . For most national team coaches, only a keeper who is playing regularly for his club merits consideration.

Unsurprisingly, Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is no exception. While he did give Urbig – the backup keeper at Bayern – two starts in his first international break as national team boss, for the upcoming UEFA Nations League matches against Serbia and the Netherlands, Marc-André ter Stegen remains the undisputed No. 1.

Sources indicate that but when Klopp gave ter Stegen the nod, Urbig was still spending most of his time on the bench in Munich. But this is set to change after Bayern's recent Bundesliga win over Mainz. The 40-year-old Manuel Neuer asked to be subbed off just before halftime, complaining of severe pain in his right foot.

An examination revealed that Neuer has sustained a partial tendon tear in the foot.

"An injury never comes at the right time, but it's part of the game," Neuer wrote on Instagram.

"I've been through this before, and I'll get through this one too. From now on: full focus on recovery. Until then, I will support the boys on the pitch wherever I can.".

It has been revealed that A partial tendon tear usually results in a layoff of six to 12 weeks, depending on the severity of the injury. Given that Neuer's foot already has some pre-existing damage from previous injuries, his recovery could take even longer.

Although Urbig is now the de-facto first-choice keeper for Bayern, he will still have to bide his time in the national team as understudy to ter Stegen. However, there is a general consensus that someday, Urbig will also become Germany's No. 1. With Neuer's contract running out in the summer, the chance to truly make the Bayern goal his own appears likely in the not-too-distant future.

Industry observers note that the match on Saturday was Neuer's 550th in the Bundesliga and he also became the oldest player in a league match in Bayern's history when he took the pitch aged 40 years and 225 days. In other words, he can't go on forever.

One of his most famous predecessors in the Bayern goal has already called on him to draw a line under his highly successful career.

"I would tell him: 'Call it a day, Manu!' You have given an incredible amount to football, you have won everything, and you don't have to prove anything to anyone anymore," Sepp Maier, a member of West Germany's 1974 World Cup winning team told Sport1.

At some point, the now 82-year-old Maier noted, there comes a moment "when your body no longer behaves the way you want it to. And even a Manuel Neuer cannot stave off that moment.".

For now, with ter Stegen playing regularly and performing well for Ajax, Germany coach Klopp is under no pressure to make a change. However, the 34-year-old former Barcelona keeper has, like Neuer, become quite injury-prone in recent years. Whenever he's needed, Urbig will be more than happy to seize his opportunity.

This article was adapted from German.

Alisson Becker (Liverpool); Ngoy (Lille), Logan Costa (Villarreal), Hermoso (Roma); Cherki (Man City), Barella (Inter), Milla (Como), Gordon (Barcelona); Bellingham (Real Madrid); Cucho Hernandez (Real Betis), Mbappé (Real Madrid).
