Sources indicate that A total of 100,000 cells from each condition were fixed with the Low Input Cell Fixation v.3 kit (Parse Biosciences, ECLC3303) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Cells were processed with the Evercode WT v.3 kit (Parse Biosciences, ECWT3300). Eight sub-libraries of 12,500 cells were generated according to manufacturer’s instructions and sequenced on an Illumina Nextseq2000 with read lengths (Read 1, 64; Read 2, 58; Index 1: 8; Index 2, 8). Sequencing data were demultiplexed and aligned to the human genome (GRCh38 Parse Biosciences) using split-pipe (v.1.6.3).

Sources indicate that raw count matrices generated by Parse Biosciences split-pipe demultiplexing were imported into R using the ReadMtx function from Seurat v.4, loading the count matrix, cell metadata and gene annotation files from the DGE_filtered directory. A Seurat object was created requiring genes detected in at least three cells and a minimum of 200 features per cell. Mitochondrial content was calculated using PercentageFeatureSet. Cells were filtered to retain those with 200–7,500 detected genes and less than 25% mitochondrial reads. Untransduced cells and two genomic coordinate-labelled perturbation conditions were excluded. Perturbation identities were mapped from sample barcodes to gene or enhancer labels, and cells were classified as non-targeting or perturbed. Gene-expression data were normalized using Seurat NormalizeData, variable features identified with FindVariableFeatures and expression values scaled with ScaleData. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on the RNA assay, followed by UMAP embedding using the top 30 principal components.

Local perturbation signatures were calculated using CalcPerturbSig from Seurat, subtracting the average expression of the k = 20 nearest non-targeting neighbour cells in PCA space (30 dimensions) to remove technical variation, producing a perturbation assay. The perturbation assay was centred, projected into PCA space using variable features from the RNA assay and visualized by UMAP. Mixscape83 was run on the scaled perturbation assay using RunMixscape with a minimum of five differentially expressed genes, ten iterations and perturbation type set to knockdown. This classified cells as knockdown, escaped or non-targeting based on posterior probability of perturbation. Escaped cells were excluded from all downstream analyses. Knockdown classification rates were computed per perturbation as the proportion of cells assigned knockdown status. Linkage disequilibrium analysis was performed on knockdown and non-targeting control cells using MixscapeLDA on the PRTB assay (ten principal components, log2[fold change] threshold 0.25) and a UMAP was computed on the top linear discriminant analysis dimensions for visualization of perturbation-specific clustering.

Differential expression between KD and non-targeting control cells was performed per perturbation using DESeq2 (v.1.52.0). Cells were assigned randomly to three pseudo-replicates within each perturbation and non-targeting control group, and raw counts were aggregated. Genes with fewer than ten total counts across pseudo-replicates were excluded. Differential expression was tested using a negative binomial model with perturbation condition as the independent variable. Results were filtered at FDR < 0.05.

Pre-ranked GSEA was performed per perturbation using fgsea (v.1.38.0) with genes ranked by log2[fold change] from DESeq2. Gene sets from MSigDB Hallmark and Gene Ontology Biological Process collections were obtained using the msigdbr (v.26.1.1) package (Homo sapiens). Minimum and maximum gene set sizes were set to 10 and 500, respectively, with 1,000 permutations. P values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg method across perturbations.

Pairwise cosine similarity was computed between the log2[fold change] vectors of all perturbations across the union of tested genes. Missing values were replaced with zero. Perturbations were clustered hierarchically on the resulting similarity matrix and visualized as a heatmap using pheatmap (v.1.0.13).

cNMF26,84 was applied to the raw count matrix of Mixscape-classified knockdown and non-targeting control cells. Counts were exported as an AnnData h5ad file and processed using the cNMF Python package (v.1.7.1). Genes expressed in fewer than five cells and all-zero genes were removed before factorization. Factorization was performed over k = 5–10 components with 100 iterations per k value and random seed 42. The optimal k = 8 was selected based on stability and reconstruction error, with a local-density threshold of 0.01 applied during consensus clustering; 99 of 800 (12%) outlier spectra were removed. Six of eight programmes were retained based on coherent gene set enrichment; two programmes dominated by unannotated loci and lacking enrichment were excluded. cNMF usage scores were imported back into R and added to the Seurat object metadata. Programme identity was assigned by over-representation analysis of the top 100 programme-specific genes against MSigDB Hallmark and Gene Ontology Biological Process gene sets using enricher from clusterProfiler (v.4.20.0).

Transcription factor motif enrichment per cNMF programme was assessed by over-representation analysis of top 100 programme genes against Gene Transcription Regulation Database transcription factor target-gene sets from MSigDB C3. Transcription factor activity was estimated using the univariate linear model method implemented in decoupleR (v.2.17.0), with the DoRothEA regulon85 (confidence levels A–C) as the prior network. cNMF gene specificity score vectors (genes × programmes) were used as input. Transcription factors with the highest variance across programmes were retained for visualization.

Industry observers note that FMC module scores were computed using AddModuleScore in Seurat on a curated list of FMC marker genes as described above. Stimulated SMC up- and down-regulated gene sets were derived from FindAllMarkers differential expression between stimulated (Zim3_3d3d) and control (Zim3_ctrl) conditions, filtered at FDR < 0.05 and |log2[fold change]| > 0.25. A signed stimulation score was computed as the difference between up- and down-regulated module scores. Spearman correlations between module scores and cNMF programme usage were computed using cor.test. Per perturbation mean scores were compared using the Wilcoxon rank sum test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. The Spearman correlation between each perturbation’s full log2[fold change] profile and the signed stimulated SMC log2[fold change] vector was computed across shared genes.

Industry observers note that RRA86 was applied across all perturbation DESeq2 gene rankings using the RobustRankAggreg (v.1.2.1) R package, separately for upregulated and down-regulated genes ranked by adjusted P value. Genes passing FDR < 0.05 after Benjamini–Hochberg correction of RRA scores were retained as the convergent programme. Each gene was assigned a direction based on the RRA result with the lower score. The top 30 convergent genes by number of perturbations in which they reached significance were selected for visualization. A convergent programme score was computed per cell as the difference between up and down module scores using AddModuleScore. Pathway enrichment of convergent up and down-regulated genes was performed using enricher against MSigDB Hallmark and GO Biological Process gene sets.

Recent findings suggest that bulk in situ Hi-C libraries for 15 different coronary artery samples across a multi-ethnic cohort were generated with the Arima Hi-C kit, according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Specifically, one Hi-C library was created from each biological sample, with an input of approximately 800,000 cells each. Restriction enzymes cutting at ^GATC and G^ANTC were used in library construction, and approximately 600 million reads were sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq 4000 per library.

In a recent development, hi-C reads were processed with the nf-core Hi-C pipeline (v.2.0.0)87 and downstream maps were analysed at 5-kb resolution. Resolution assessment, library quality metrics, loop-caller benchmarking, inherent normalization and visualization procedures88,89 are described in Supplementary Figs. 5–7. Phased contact matrices using sample-specific genotypes were processed using Axiotl’s Turnkey platform (tinker.axiotl.com), which leverages Hi-C-Pro v.3.1.0 and cloud compute.

Sources indicate that we called cohort-specific 3D structures using the AQuA Tools framework90 for 3D genomics. Sample-wise chromatin structures were called in BEDPE format using extract_bedpe. We used union_bedpe to stack and merge BEDPE coordinates coming from various samples into one BEDPE file that contained the union set coordinates of all possible Hi-C connections in the cohort. This allowed for resolving overlapping interactions and outputting a common scaffold. To assign membership (as unique identifiers to column 7) to the stacked loops based on shared overlap of BEDPE anchors, we used cluster_bedpe. This resulting file became the mosaic for the cohort. To assess their functional and disease relevance, we intersected two-dimensional mosaic coordinates with one-dimensional genomic features including genes and snATAC peaks harbouring CAD GWAS variants. Against the mosaic BEDPE, contact values for each sample were queried in inherent and counts per million (CPM) numeric spaces using query_bedpe. All downstream analyses were performed in R.

In a recent development, all experiments were performed on primary HCASMC between passages 4 and 7. Antibodies used for ChIP–qPCR were all pre-validated according to ChIP–seq guidelines. Purified rabbit monoclonal antibody against human CTCF (Abcam, ab128873; clone EPR7314(B)). Cell lines with various genotypes of rs4887091 were used. Approximately 2 × 106 HCASMC for each line were fixed with 1% formaldehyde and quenched by glycine. The cells were washed three times with PBS and then harvested in ChIP lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8, 5 mM EDTA, 0.5% SDS). Crosslinked chromatin was sheared for 2 × 1 min by sonication (Branson SFX250 Sonifier) before extensive centrifugation. Four volumes of ChIP dilution buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 2 mM EDTA, 1% Triton X-100) was added to the supernatant. The resulting lysate was then incubated with Dynabeads Protein G (Thermo Scientific, 10009D) and antibodies at 4 °C overnight. Beads were washed once with buffer 1 (20 mM Tris pH 8, 2 mM EDTA, 150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS), once with buffer 2 (10 mM Tris pH 8, 1 mM EDTA, 500 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS), once with buffer 3 (10 mM Tris pH 8, 1 mM EDTA, 250 mM LiCl, 1% NP40, 1% sodium deoxycholate monohydrate) and twice with TE buffer. DNA was eluted by ChIP elution buffer (0.1 M NaHCO3, 1% SDS, 20 μg ml−1 proteinase K). The elution was incubated at 65 °C overnight, and DNA was extracted with a DNA purification kit (Zymo, D4013). The purified DNA from various lines were analysed by qPCR using the ABI ViiA 7, with the same primer applied to each SNP. Assays were repeated at least three times. Data are average values ± s.d. of representative experiments.

CAD-associated variants were represented as 1-bp genomic intervals (hg38) and intersected with HCASMC CTCF ChIP–seq peak intervals. Observed overlap was defined as the number of CAD variants overlapping at least one CTCF peak. To estimate overlap expected by chance while preserving genomic structure, we performed chromosome-wise circular permutation of CTCF peak coordinates. For each chromosome, peak start coordinates were shifted by a random offset uniformly sampled from \([1,L-1]\), where L is chromosome length, with wraparound at chromosome boundaries. Peak widths and chromosome assignments were preserved. For each of B = 1,000 permutations, we recalculated the number of CAD variants overlapping permuted CTCF peaks to generate an empirical null distribution.

Fold enrichment was calculated as.

Empirical one-sided P values were computed as.

For parametric approximation, we set \({p}_{0}\) to the null mean overlap probability (mean(null overlaps)/N) and computed the exact one-sided binomial probability of observing \(\ge \)k overlaps among N variants.

According to recent reports, enriched and input DNA were quantified by SYBR Green qPCR on ViiA 7. In addition to SYBR Green primers, we also used TaqMan genotyping probe (ThermoFisher, AN7EEGX, lot no. P260615-009) to directly amplify the different alleles of the DNA in heterozygous lines. Relative CTCF enrichment for target (rs4887091) and control loci was calculated as percent input. Target allele-specific binding effects were confirmed by benchmarking enrichment profiles against the expected quantitative gradients of the in-house validated allelic controls.

To identify endogenous allelic controls across the four cell lines, CTCF ChIP–seq peaks were intersected with corresponding whole-genome sequencing VCF files. SNPs exhibiting complete genotypic gradients (homozygous reference, heterozygous, homozygous alternative) were scored for CTCF motif perturbation using the JASPAR matrix (MA0139.2). Allelic positive controls were defined by severe motif disruption (\(\Delta \text{Score}\ge 6.0\), max score \( > 8.0\)), whereas negative controls exhibited preserved motif integrity (\(\Delta \text{Score}\le 0.2\), both scores \( > 8.0\)).

Sources indicate that to prevent cross-cell-line amplification bias, SYBR Green qPCR primers (75–150 bp amplicons) were designed using Primer3 v.2.6.1. An in silico masking pipeline strictly discarded any candidate primer pairs whose binding sites overlapped with endogenous variants in the merged four-cell-line VCF, ensuring 100% conserved annealing kinetics across all biological samples.

Hi-ChIP was adapted from previously published protocols with some modifications91,92. Briefly, at least 1 million healthy HCASMCs (Thermo Scientific, C-017-5C, lot no. 1689414) and healthy HCAECs (ATCC, PCS-100-020, lot no. 62382179) were crosslinked with 1% formaldehyde. The initial Hi-C portion followed the Arima Hi-C protocol described in the Arima High Coverage Hi-C Kit (Arima Genomics, A410110). For the immunoprecipitation step, sheared chromatin after the Hi-C portion of the protocol was immunoprecipitated with 5 μg of H3K27ac antibody (Abcam, ab4729) with 50 μl of protein G Dynabeads (Invitrogen 10004D) and allowed to incubate overnight at 4 °C. The protein G Dynabeads were washed and the immunoprecipitated DNA was de-crosslinked at 67 °C for 2 h and eluted (50 mM sodium bicarbonate, 1% SDS). Subsequently, Dynabeads MyOne Streptavidin C1 beads (Invitrogen, 65002) were used to enrich ligated junctions as per Hi-C protocol. Library preparation was performed using the NEB Ultra II library preparation kit (NEB, E7645L), according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Twelve PCR cycles were performed using indexed primers and subsequently DNA fragments between 300 bp and 500 bp were size selected using the Omega MagBind NGS clean up Magnetic beads (Omega, M1378). The libraries were sequenced by paired-end sequencing with at least 300 million read pairs at 2 × 151-bp read length on Illumina HiSeq 4000 platforms. Raw paired-end reads in Fastq format for respective samples were processed using the Hi-CuP pipeline93 (v.0.7.4). The hg38 human genome was used as reference to generate the Hi-CuP Digest file using two restriction motifs GATC and GANTC using the hicup_digester command for running the Hi-CuP pipeline. Paired contacts were extracted from aligned filtered bam files using Samtools (v.1.13) and used as input for the pre function in the Juicer package to generate hic files94. Paired interaction counts at 5 kb resolution were extracted from the matrix, and high-confidence chromatin loops were identified using the FitHiChIP tool (v.11.0) as described previously using default parameters95. Using HCASMC and HCAEC ChIP–seq peak files as input, and initial paired interaction files, high-confidence peak-to-all interactions with a 5-kb bin size were processed using the bash FitHiChIP_HiCPro.sh script (https://ay-lab.github.io/FitHiChIP/). High-confidence chromatin interactions were sorted and indexed in bed format and converted to long-range format for visualization on the WashU browser. The overlay of Hi-ChIP, ChIP–seq and GWAS data was plotted using the locuszoomr package (v.0.3.5) and R (v.4.3.1).

ChIP–seq was performed as described previously with minor optimizations96. Briefly, 1 million HCASMCs and HCAECs from the same lot used for Hi-ChIP experiments were crosslinked with 1% formaldehyde for 10 min at room temperature and quenched with glycine (125 mM) for 5 min. The cells were rinsed twice with cold 1× PBS and sonicated in nuclei lysis buffer (50 mM HEPES–KOH, pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1% Triton X, 0.1% sodium deoxycholate, 1% SDS, Takara, 1× protease inhibitor) using the Bioruptor sonicator to obtain chromatin fragments between 200 bp and 500 bp. The fragmented chromatin was immunoprecipitated overnight at 4 °C, with 5 μg of H3K27ac antibody (Abcam, ab4729) and 50 μl of protein G beads (Invitrogen, 10004D). Subsequently, the beads were washed and immunoprecipitated DNA was de-crosslinked and eluted in elution buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, and 10 mM EDTA). Eluted ChIP fragments were isolated using phenol–chloroform extraction method, and DNA was purified by ethanol precipitation. Library preparation was performed on the eluted ChIP DNA using the NEB Ultra II library preparation kit, according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Ten PCR cycles were performed using indexed primers and the library of DNA fragments with sizes between 300 bp and 500 bp was selected using the Omega MagBind NGS clean up Magnetic beads (Omega, M1378). The libraries were sent for paired-end sequencing, with at least 50 million read pairs at 2 × 151-bp read length on the Illumina HiSeq 4000 platform. Paired-end sequencing reads were aligned to human genome (hg38) using BWA mem v.0.7.5 (ref. 97), and reads were deduplicated using Picard v.3.4.0 MarkDuplicates. Aligned mapped reads in BAM file were used as input for peak-calling using Dfilter98 to identify significant H3K27ac peaks using the following setting: -ks = 60, -bs = 100, -Ipvalue = 8. Bigwig tracks were normalized for sequencing depths and the sum of normalized binned tag-count represents the peak height.

Healthy HCASMCs (Thermo Scientific, C-017-5C, lot no. 1689414) were cultured in human vascular smooth muscle basal medium (Gibco, M231500), in Smooth Muscle Growth Supplement (Gibco, S00725) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. Healthy HCAECs (ATCC, PCS-100-020, lot no. 62382179) were cultured in Endothelial Cell Growth medium MV2 (PromoCell, C-22022).

Zhang (Addgene, 52963, LentiGuide-Puro) in which the non-targeting control sgRNAs and sgRNAs targeting the TSS and regulatory enhancer were annealed and ligated into the Esp3I cut-site of the Lentiguide-Puro vector using T4 Ligase (NEB, M0202) as per the manufacturer’s instructions. Ligation products were transformed into One Shot Stbl3 Chemically competent Escherichia coli (Invitrogen, C737303) and plasmids of positive clones were isolated using FavorPrep Plasmid DNA Extract Kit (Favorgen, FAPDE001-1). Medium was refreshed overnight with reduced 5% FBS in DMEM medium, and the expended medium was collected twice after 24 h and 48 h, respectively. Pooled supernatant was filtered through a polyethersulfone 0.45 μm filter and viral particles were concentrated using Viro-PEG Lentivirus Concentrator (Ozbiosciences, LVG100) as per the manufacturer’s instructions.

Healthy HCASMCs (Thermo Scientific, C-017-5C, lot no. 1689414) and HCAECs (ATCC, PCS-100-020, lot no. 62382179) were both co-transduced in 5 μg ml−1 polybrene with lentiviral particles packaged from Lenti-dCas9-KRAB-blast (Addgene, 89567)99, and individual sgRNAs were cloned into Lentiguide-Puro backbone (Addgene, 52963)100 at a multiplicity of infection of 3. Respective HCASMC and HCAEC growth media were refreshed after 24 h of infection, and co-selection with 10 μg ml−1 blasticidin (Gibco, A1113903) and 1 μg ml−1 puromycin (Gibco, A1113803) was performed 72 h following infection. Selected cells were allowed to recover and expanded for 2 weeks before RNA isolation using Trizol Reagent (Gibco, 15596026) and Direct-Zol RNA miniprep (Zymo Research, R2052) as per the manufacturer’s instructions. cDNA conversion was performed with at least 200 ng RNA using HiScript III RT SuperMix (Vazyme Biotech, R323-01), and reverse transcription-PCR was performed using gene-specific primers to assess for gene expression.

The following reverse transcription-PCR primers were used:.

AMOTL2_F: 5′-AGTGAGCGACAAACAGCAGACG-3′.

AMOTL2_R: 5′-ATCTCTGCTCCCGTGTTTGGCA-3′.

GAPDH_F: 5′-GTGGACCTGACCTGCCGTCT-3′.

GAPDH_R: 5′-GGAGGAGTGGGTGTCGCTGT-3′.

PPIA_F: 5′-CACCGTGTTCTTCGACATTG-3′.

PPIA_R: 5′-TTCTGCTGTCTTTGGGACCT-3′.

Sources indicate that cell kinetic proliferation live-cell imaging was performed using the HoloMonitor M4 system (Phase Holographic Imaging, PHI AB) using the Cell Kinetic Proliferation assay protocol as per the manufacturer’s instructions. Non-targeting controls and AMOTL2 dCas9-KRAB CRISPRi knockdown HCASMCs were seeded and cultured in vascular smooth muscle cell medium, in smooth muscle growth supplement, at a confluence of 15,000 cells cm−2 in a 24-well vessel (VWR, 734-2325) (n = 8). The 24-well HoloLid (PHI AB, 71130) was used to enhance the visualization and tracking of cells. At least five capture areas were taken per well, and time-lapse imaging at every 30-min time interval was taken across wells over 72 h. Cellular segmentation was performed using the HoloMonitor App Suite (v.3.5.2.446). Cellular confluence was captured and normalized to baseline at 0 h.

It has been revealed that total RNA was extracted using Trizol Reagent (ThermoFisher, 15596026) and Direct-Zol RNA miniprep Kit (Zymo Research, R2050). At least three independent replicates were used for RNA library preparations. RNA quality and yield was assessed using Agilent RNA 6000 pico kit (Agilent, 5067-1513) for quality. Bulk RNA-seq library preparations were prepared using VAHTS Universal V10 RNA-seq Library Prep Kit for Illumina (Vazyme, NR606-01) with Ribodepletion, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. cDNA libraries were prepared using Illumina RNA Truseq indexes and quantified using Agilent Tapestation. Sequencing was performed on the NovaSeq X Plus (PE150) by NovogeneAIT Singapore, yielding 50 million raw pair-end reads. Raw Fastq files were trimmed using the trim-galore tool (v.0.65) from Babraham Bioinformatics to sequence length of 50. Paired-end reads were mapped and aligned to the human reference genome GRCh38–hg38 using STAR aligner (v.2.7.0) as per default settings and using gene annotations from GENCODE v.38. Aligned gene counts were mapped using HTSeq-count v.2.1.2 and normalized to TPM by sequencing depth and by gene length. Differential gene-expression analysis was performed using EdgeR (v.3.42.4). Contrasts were compared between non-targeting control and AMOTL2 TSS knockdown cells. A negative binomial generalized log-linear model was used to model gene counts using the glmFit function. |log[fold change]| >0.5 and FDR < 0.05 cut-offs were used to identify significantly differentially expressed genes following multiple testing correction. Figures were generated with R v.3.5.1.

It has been revealed that HCASMCs were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (ThermoFisher, 5090495) for 15 min at room temperature, then washed with 3× PBS for 5 min at room temperature. Cells were permeabilized with PBS with 0.1% Triton X-100 for 15 min, followed by blocking in 5% normal goat serum in PBS (blocking buffer) for 1 h at room temperature. Primary anti-Calponin (1:100) (ProteinTech, 13938-1-AP), and primary anti-α-smooth muscle actin antibody (1:100) (Sigma-Aldrich, A5228) were diluted in blocking buffer and added to permeabilized cells overnight at 4 °C. After washing with PBS three times for 5 min, cells were incubated with Alexa fluor-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:1,000) (Goat anti-mouse 594, ThermoFisher, A-11032; goat anti-rabbit 488, ThermoFisher, A-11008) and 1 μg ml−1 DAPI for 1 h at room temperature. Stained cells were washed three times for 5 min each with PBS, and images were acquired under the same laser exposure and magnification using a fluorescence microscope (EVOS M7000).

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Raw and processed sequencing files can be found as follows: Human Coronary Multi-ome: GSE328800. Human Coronary Hi-C: GSE328970. Genotyping for Human Samples: dbGaP accession ID phs004118.v1.p1. HCASMC Perturb–seq: GSE347104. CTCF ChIP–seq in HCASMCs: GSE319778. H3K27ac/Hi-ChIP in HCASMC and HCAEC: GSE282556 and GSE282557. Bulk RNA-seq AMOTL2: GSE329169. Public and/or reference resources used in this study include GTEx v.8, the 1000 Genomes Project Phase 3 reference panel and the GRCh38–hg38 human reference genome. Previously published datasets used for validation or reference mapping include GSE131780, GSE175621 and GSE188422.

Scripts used for analysis in this manuscript can be found at GitHub (https://github.com/jamrute/CAD-scV2E2G).

Germany slips in climate protection rankings as other countries make gains

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Germany has slipped down the climate action ranking for the third consecutive year, with the former green leader now being outperformed by Brazil, Colombia and Romania.
  • In its worst performance since 2019, the country fell to place 25 and received a "medium" rating overall on the yearly Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI), which assesses efforts to curb global warming in 64 countries plus the European Union.
  • It has been revealed that still, "a number of countries have been making good progress for years," said Jan Burck, CCPI lead author, in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Germany has slipped down the climate action ranking for the third consecutive year, with the former green leader now being outperformed by Brazil, Colombia and Romania.

In its worst performance since 2019, the country fell to place 25 and received a "medium" rating overall on the yearly Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI), which assesses efforts to curb global warming in 64 countries plus the European Union.

It has been revealed that still, "a number of countries have been making good progress for years," said Jan Burck, CCPI lead author, in a statement. Denmark is leading the way across all four categories assessed — energy use, greenhouse gas emissions, renewable energy and national climate policy. A total of 15 states, including Lithuania, Chile, and Morocco, received an overall "high" rating, which is two more than last year.

The European Union also moved up a spot, while Hungary jumped 21 places after the ousting of former prime minister Viktor Orban's government, which had repeatedly vetoed EU climate intends, dismissing them as a "utopian fantasy.".

The top three positions on the CCPI remained vacant again this year, as no country has yet done enough to meet global climate goals aimed at preventing worsening weather extremes and climate damage.

Sources indicate that "We are seeing a striking contrast," said Burck. "Progress on climate action is often slow and in some countries, such as the United States, things are even moving backwards. But technologically and economically there is enormous momentum.".

That momentum is apparent in record solar energy growth. Last year 75% of global electricity demand growth was met by the green energy source, according to energy think tank Ember's latest global electricity review. Investment in clean energy has also outpaced that in fossil fuels for multiple years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The rapid expansion of renewable technology, as well as the Iran War and a reduction in deforestation are behind a projected slight fall in emissions for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the CCPI.

"Governments have to act now to turn the momentum into sustained emissions reductions," said CCPI co-author Niklas Höhne of the NewClimate Institute, which compiles the report with environmental NGO Germanwatch.

Burck attributed Germany's worst ever performance in the category of national climate policy to current policies being pursued by Germany's economy minister Katherina Reiche.

"Measures that primarily aim to increase the use of natural gas, threaten to undermine progress in the energy transition and risk significantly worsening the conditions for renewable energy and electrification for many years to come," mentioned Burck.

A European Commission report published on November 9 on the sidelines of the UN COP31 climate summit in Turkey remarked Germany was one of nine EU countries set to miss 2030 emissions reductions targets.

Sources indicate that germany is not alone in its disappointing ranking. The other G20 countries — the world's leading industrialized and emerging economies, responsible for around 80% of global CO2 emissions — also perform poorly.

The only exception among them is the United Kingdom, which ranks seventh and received a high rating, performing well in greenhouse gas emissions, energy use and climate policy. However, study authors rated it low for renewable energy expansion.

The G20's oil- and gas-producing countries occupy some of the lowest positions on the climate action table. The United States, which is the world's second largest emitter, languishes alongside Russia, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Canada around the bottom of the league, with an overall rating of "very low.".

According to recent reports, the hosts of this year's COP31, also received a "low" overall score. Australia, a major coal exporter with some of the world's highest per-capita emissions, ranks 54th, while Turkey, which is also heavily dependent on fossil fuels, comes in 53rd.

China is the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases and ranks 56th in the CCPI, receiving an overall rating of "very low." Its main weaknesses include its now high per-capita emissions and substantial energy consumption.

However, among the G20, China leads the way in renewable energy expansion. The country, which is five years ahead of schedule in reaching its goal of adding 1,200 GW of wind and solar capacity to the grid by 2030, also produces over 80% of the world's solar panels.

Several oil-producing countries, including Kazakhstan, Saudi Arabia, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates, are also performing better than expected in the renewables category and "are significantly expanding their previously limited" capacity, said the report.

The authors said these countries have significant potential to further expand renewables.

In a recent development, "In the Arab states in particular, very high per-capita emissions and an above-average level of electrification coincide with a relatively low existing share of renewable energy and enormous solar potential," mentioned co-author Natalie Pelekh in a statement. "These are, in fact, ideal conditions for more ambitious climate action.".

When England and Manchester United defender Harry Maguire finally decides to hang up his boots, he may have an alternative to the pundits’ studio.

Maguire, 33, is co-founder of a upcoming AI coaching app, Feedz, that is already transforming the way elite sports teams are instructing their talent with their cutting-edge voice-to-report technology.

The Manchester United centre-half started the organization alongside British tech entrepreneur Matt White in May and the app is already being used by sporting outfits, including Maguire's club United, Chelsea's women's team and Sunderland.

Having bounced back from setbacks and criticism throughout his career, Maguire's resilience will stand him in good stead if he decides to transition from the backline to the touchline.

And while it is not a traditional managerial role his decision demonstrates a keen eye on the future of coaching and the development of young athletes.

A lot of new AI developments are mind-boggling on the face of it, but what sets Feedz apart is just how easy it is to use.

Harry Maguire has co-founded the revolutionary new AI coaching app, Feedz.

All a coach needs to do is dictate a messy audio message giving instructions to a player and within seconds Feedz will provide them with a PDF outlining exactly where their player is succeeding, where they must improve and how to do it.

Even more impressive, the use of this app is not limited to football and indeed has fast become a tool used all over the globe in 19 different sports.

Feedz has also been able to cross the Atlantic, with the technology being used by a plethora of elite institutions across the pond – most notably Sporting Jacksonville, who, with more than 150 coaches training 10,000 young players, are the largest soccer academy in the States and something of a feeder club for top MLS teams.

Co-founder Matt White tells Daily Mail Sport: 'The purpose of Feedz is to develop youth sports. There is no downside to feedback, transparency between coach, player and parent is the flywheel.

'The concern is time. Coaches don’t have the time to give feedback consistently, the technology now exists to solve that problem of time. Coaches can now give feedback in seconds.

According to recent reports, 'This is across all sports. Caroline Elite, a US soccer academy in the US, have over 2,000 players... it used to take them two weeks to give feedback to these players and  now it takes two hours.'.

White then emphasised the vast number of sports in which Feedz can be used, and outlined the elite outfits already using it.

'Feedz is for all sports,' he states. 'Multiple schools, cricket counties like Surrey, Sussex, Kent, Glamorgan, Middlesex. Table Tennis England, Sale Sharks rugby club, Surbiton hockey club, Sunderland AFC, Manchester United, West Riding Oxfordshire (riding club), Louisiana Fire, Arizona Arsenal, Sporting Iowa (US soccer teams), Soccer Indiana. They all use Feedz.

Sources indicate that 'Good feedback helps a young player understand what they’re doing well and what to work on. It also helps parents feel involved and gives coaches a way to track progress over time.'.

Another encouraging aspect of Feedz is that the tech giant aims to help young sportspeople at all levels of the game.

White explains that when he started the firm he went straight to the FA's head of grassroots football to ensure that coaches who simply don't have the time or resources to relay meaningful feedback to their players could do so.

His savvy investment may point to Maguire's plans post-retirement.

He went on to explain that at the highest level professional athletes have nutritionists, personal physios and all of the available data handed to them to ensure they can perform at their best but young talent are often not given the same chance to reach their potential.

Maguire told White: 'This is the exact kind of thing I would have loved to have as a young player coming through.'.

In a world where the majority of stories on AI are negative and inspire fear, this is a use of the technology that can keep grassroots football alive and even help it thrive.

And, just as he approaches the twilight of his own career, Maguire clearly agrees.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for the first time in 616 days, Tottenham Hotspur have won three Premier League matches in a row. Three different managers have been sacked in that time, and the mood in north London had plunged to grim lows, but finally there is a sense that something truly exciting is stirring at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

Recent findings suggest that this victory over Crystal Palace was not as impressive as last week’s triumph at Chelsea, but it did not need to be. After Palace striker Jean-Philippe Mateta was sent off in the 13th minute, Spurs simply had to make their numerical advantage count. They did so with relative ease, taking complete control of possession and creating endless goalscoring opportunities.

Roberto De Zerbi’s team ended the night with 34 shots to Palace’s two and with 758 completed passes to Palace’s 149. The goals ultimately came from two defenders, Archie Gray and Jan Paul van Hecke, but there was a long list of Spurs players who might have scored here.

It has been revealed that spurs take the lead through an Archie Gray header! ⚪ https://t.co/qSCECkOJur.

Did this defeat mark the end for Pierre Sage, the Palace manager? The Frenchman was only appointed in June but it has been a grisly start to the campaign. Palace have the worst defence in the league, have lost six of nine games and have not produced any truly encouraging performances in the Premier League.

Even in the two games Palace have won, against Fulham and Nottingham Forest, they were lucky to do so. The likes of Sean Dyche and Thomas Frank, both of whom would be strong candidates to replace Sage if Palace do pull the trigger, will no doubt have been keeping an eye on events here.

“I am really aware of the situation,” Sage noted. “I don’t like this situation. [But] you can trust in me, I will never give up. I want to be the first on the pitch on Monday. I have the rage to train more. It’s not me to decide this thing [his future]. If I have one hour, I will give my best for one hour. If I have 10 years, I will give my best for 10 years.”.

In a recent development, the decision for Palace chairman Steve Parish, then, is whether this result represented a continuation of the team’s problems or was an aberration caused by the early red card. It would be reasonable for Sage to claim this match was out of his hands from the moment Mateta lunged at Spurs captain Micky van de Ven, but such an argument might not carry much weight with Palace sitting 18th in the table.

The challenge was foolish in the extreme by Mateta, a player who was much more successful in exiting this game than he has been in his numerous attempts to leave Palace in recent transfer windows. At first glance it did not seem the worst tackle, but the replays were damning: Mateta led with his studs and made forceful contact with Van de Ven’s ankle.

Sources indicate that it was an inexcusably brainless act, after just 13 minutes of play, and the same could be said of Palace’s defending from a right-wing corner a few minutes later. Mohammed Kudus swirled the delivery to the back post, where Gray was unmarked. Yes, Palace were defending with 10. But no, that does not justify the inability of Sage’s players to spot Gray. Even more embarrassingly, the Tottenham player was unmarked again from another corner shortly afterwards.

It was not the first time this season that Palace’s cause has been undermined by a red card. When they lost at home to Ipswich Town in September, Axel Disasi was sent off after 34 minutes. An absence of discipline? Perhaps. Sage might argue, though, that he is not responsible for his players demonstrating a lack of basic brainpower.

Jean-Philippe Mateta receives his first red card for Crystal Palace! 🟥 https://t.co/U9UYb29mbk.

Recent findings suggest that all of this was welcomed heartily by the Spurs fans, who celebrated Mateta’s dismissal as though it was a goal. Recent results have restored some of the enthusiasm in this corner of north London and the mood here was buoyant, even before Gray’s opener.

“Now we are playing as a team,” De Zerbi stated. “Before the international break, we were playing as many good players but not as a team. We revealed our maturity. We are improving.”.

Industry observers note that the second goal was always coming and it arrived in the 73rd minute, when Van Hecke attacked a wonderful cross by Mateus Fernandes. Palace goalkeeper Dean Henderson saved the first attempt but the ball dropped onto the head of Van Hecke, now seated in the six-yard box, and he happily nodded it home.

In a recent development, spurs face Leeds United, Ipswich Town, Sunderland and Fulham in their next four league games. The momentum could, and perhaps should, continue to build. Their optimism here contrasted sharply with the angst of Palace, and with the troubled look that was etched on Sage’s face.

“Very pleased for the performance, very tough game. You don’t know 11 [against 11] would be different game but Crystal Palace are very tough because they defend with a low block, no space and we revealed we are a mature team. Maybe we could score more goals with more nastiness, but I am very happy because we created many chances. We need more goals for sure. It’s not enough, but we are improving a lot.

It has been revealed that “I was very nervous before the game, during the game, after the red card, it’s always better playing with one player more. But today, against this team, they played with this behaviour, all behind the line of the ball, aggressive. Very tough game.”.

According to recent reports, when asked if Spurs are looking up the table, he replied: “We don’t forget the ambitions. We have to look behind what was the situation two weeks ago. In the last two years, two times 17th in the table, many games without a win in front of our fans. We have to stay focused. They are improving, increasing the level of performance.”.

According to recent reports, speaking to Sky Sports, the Palace defender stated: “Definitely was frustrating. It was one of the first tackles of the game. And we felt like we were doing well and it is unfortunate. We go again.

“The main message was don’t concede again, stay tight as a defence and try to hit them on the counter. That is the best plan when you’re down a man.

It has been revealed that “Unfortunately, it didn’t happen today. We know what we can do as a team, as a back five, the whole unit. There were some positives in the games, but I can’t say much when you lose. We just have to go again.

According to recent reports, “Hopefully, the next game we win. The main message is to stay together as a team. We know what we are capable of. It is staying confident and bouncing back.”.

By BEN WILLCOCKS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR and CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 04:00 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 06:54 EST, 26 November 2026.

Manchester United legend Peter Schmeichel fears Senne Lammens has yet to recover from the blunder he made during Belgium's World Cup campaign last summer.

Lammens made two costly mistakes in United’s 2-2 Champions League draw with Sporting Lisbon on Wednesday night, conceding a needless penalty and dropping a clanger in the dying minutes to allow Luis Suarez to score twice for the home side.

The 24-year-old goalkeeper, who was one of Manchester United's standout performers last season following his £18.1million transfer from Royal Antwerp, has looked unconvincing so far this term and played a part in the club conceding more goals (35) than any other side in Europe's top five leagues.

Former Red Devils goalkeeper Schmeichel believes Lammens has never fully recovered from his error that led to Belgium being dumped out by Spain at the World Cup quarter-final stage last summer.

In the 88th minute of the match, with the score locked at 1-1, Lammens spilled the ball into the path of Mikel Merino, who tapped home to send Spain through to the semi-finals.

Asked if the confidence-shot goalkeeper should now be dropped by Mauricio Pochettino for Karl Darlow, who was signed by United in the summer, Schmeichel told CBS Sports: ‘I don’t know where that point is.

Senne Lammens made two big errors during Manchester United's 2-2 draw at Sporting Lisbon.

Peter Schmeichel fears Lammens has never fully recovered from his blunder at the World Cup.

‘Mauricio Pochettino has come in, he’s brought his own staff, that means he’s got a fresh goalkeeping coach and maybe that is something that can change it for him.

‘I don’t know if you remember in the World Cup, he came against Spain and made a bit of a mistake, Merino scored and they got knocked out, and I feel like he’s lost a little bit of confidence from that mistake, hasn’t really recovered.

‘As a goalkeeper when you’re not on your best form you need your defenders in front of you to help you out and the sad truth is that they haven’t been able to do that and of course, that makes it so much worse.'.

Joshua Zirkzee insists United’s players will rally around Lammens and won’t let their under-fire goalkeeper ‘suffer by himself’.

The two costly errors undid Lammens’ good work after he saved an earlier penalty from Suarez, but Zirkzee remarked the players are determined to support the Belgian.

‘This team is a family, so there's no one who will suffer by themselves,’ said Zirkzee. ‘Mistakes happen. Let's go on to the next one. Senne’s a great goalkeeper.

‘In this moment, we just give him space. I’m not sure if he wants to hear anything at all. But Senne’s a great kid. He's got a good head on him and we all know that next game he is going to be at the top of his game. We didn't draw because of him. I'm also someone who likes to look at myself and, you know, I didn't score.’.

United had two goals disallowed by Polish referee Szymon Marciniak as well as conceding the two penalties and seeing Youri Tielemans sent off – three days after Leny Yoro was shown a controversial red card at Liverpool – and Zirkzee admitted that it feels like the world is against Pochettino’s team at the moment.

The Belgian shot-stopper conceded a needless penalty just minutes after saving a spot-kick.

He then spilled the ball into the path of Luis Suarez late on, gifting Sporting a late equaliser.

‘Yeah, we're in a place where it can feel like that pretty quick,’ he added. ‘But as I said, we've got a locker-room that's built on supporting each other and we will get out of it eventually. If it's us against the world, so be it.

‘For the team that we are, we shouldn't really be looking at what the referee decides, but you cannot deny that it was some key decisions that weren't in our favour, to put it like that.

‘But, as I noted, we shouldn't really be looking at the referee. All we have to do is look at ourselves. In the end, I think we drew because of small details, little mistakes. But we definitely have something to build on, mainly the way we started the second half. I think that's something we can build on and move on with. Our team should be capable to win even if we're not being favoured in those moments.’.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Liverpool City Council has approved an updated Liverpool Waters masterplan, marking another significant milestone in the regeneration of the city’s northern waterfront and building on the transformation brought about by the development of Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium.
  • The revised planning framework, brought forward by Peel Waters, will guide the next phase of development across the 60-hectare site stretching from Everton's headquarters at The Royal Liver Building to the Club’s new waterfront home at Bramley-Moore Dock.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that liverpool City Council has approved an updated Liverpool Waters masterplan, marking another significant milestone in the regeneration of the city’s northern waterfront and building on the transformation brought about by the development of Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium. The revised planning framework, brought forward by Peel Waters, will guide the next phase of development across the 60-hectare site stretching from Everton's headquarters at The Royal Liver Building to the Club’s latest waterfront home at Bramley-Moore Dock. The development of Hill Dickinson Stadium has acted as a catalyst for the regeneration of North Liverpool, stimulating investment, creating employment opportunities, attracting visitors and unlocking the potential of a previously underutilised area of the city. The updated masterplan reflects the significant changes that have taken place along Liverpool’s waterfront since the original planning consent was granted in 2013, most notably the development of Everton’s new home and its emergence as a major sporting, entertainment and visitor destination. The refreshed intends will support the delivery of new homes, including affordable housing, alongside high-quality public spaces, healthcare provision, community facilities, employment opportunities and sustainable infrastructure across five distinctive waterfront neighbourhoods. Central to the plans is the creation of a new five-acre waterfront park at Central Docks. Already under construction as part of Liverpool Waters’ £81 million infrastructure investment programme, the park will feature more than 3,000 trees and is expected to open in spring 2028. The park and wider development will provide new and enhanced pedestrian routes through the northern docks, offering supporters and visitors an optional attractive walking route between Liverpool city centre and Hill Dickinson Stadium. Alongside new leisure and hospitality destinations, the creation of these public spaces will help transform the matchday and non-matchday journey for Evertonians, providing more opportunities for supporters to spend time along the waterfront before and after fixtures and major events at the stadium. The increased focus on pedestrian connectivity, active travel and sustainable transport also complements Everton’s ongoing work with key stakeholders to improve accessibility to Hill Dickinson Stadium and better connect the Club’s waterfront home with the city centre and surrounding communities.Colin Chong, Everton’s Chief Real Estate and Regeneration Officer, stated: “From the outset, our ambition for Hill Dickinson Stadium extended far beyond delivering a new home for Everton Football Club. It was also about unlocking the potential of Liverpool’s northern waterfront and providing a catalyst for wider investment, regeneration and economic growth. “We are already seeing the positive impact of the stadium on the surrounding area, with new businesses establishing themselves and existing businesses benefiting from increased footfall and activity. “The updated Liverpool Waters masterplan provides an opportunity to build on that momentum. New public spaces, improved walking routes and better connectivity will complement our own investment in establishing Hill Dickinson Stadium and our Budweiser Plaza as a year-round destination, enhancing the appeal of the area, attracting more visitors and creating further opportunities for businesses, investment and employment across North Liverpool.” The growing programme of major sporting and entertainment events at Hill Dickinson Stadium is extending the economic benefits of Everton’s investment beyond football matchdays and across the wider Liverpool City Region. As well as being the home for Everton's Premier League fixtures, Hill Dickinson Stadium has already hosted an international football fixture between Scotland and Côte d’Ivoire, a Rugby League Ashes Test, Magic WKND and a Rugby Union Nations Championship fixture, the stadium will also host matches during UEFA EURO 2028, with a programme of major concerts at the Club’s waterfront home set to get under way in summer 2027. The ability to attract events of national and international significance is helping to further strengthen Liverpool’s reputation as a global sporting, cultural and entertainment destination, drawing additional visitors to the city, supporting its hotel, hospitality, retail and transport sectors, and creating further opportunities for investment and employment across the region. Since the original Liverpool Waters masterplan was approved in 2013, the northern waterfront has undergone significant change, with the delivery of new residential developments, transport infrastructure, leisure and hospitality destinations and public spaces, alongside Hill Dickinson Stadium and the Isle of Man Ferry Terminal. James Whittaker, Managing Director of Peel Waters, said: “The approval of the updated Liverpool Waters masterplan marks another major milestone in the transformation of Liverpool’s northern waterfront. Since the original masterplan was approved in 2013, we have delivered significant progress across the site, including new homes, public spaces, leisure destinations, major transport infrastructure and the new Everton Stadium, helping establish Liverpool Waters as one of the UK’s most ambitious regeneration projects. “This updated framework reflects the considerable investment already made by Peel Waters and our partners, while providing the flexibility needed to respond to evolving market demand and future opportunities. With over £81 million of infrastructure investment committed at Central Docks, Princes Dock nearing completion and a clear vision for future neighbourhoods, Liverpool Waters is entering an exciting new chapter that will continue to create homes, jobs, investment and opportunities for Liverpool and the wider city region.” The revised framework also strengthens commitments around sustainability, biodiversity, climate resilience and the preservation of Liverpool’s rich maritime heritage – principles that were central to the development of Everton’s waterfront home. Pete Swift, CEO and Co-Founder, Planit – the landscape architecture, urban design and masterplanning studio who also worked as part of the team to deliver Everton's new home, added: “We are overjoyed at the approval, not just for the Peel Waters and Liverpool Waters team but for the communities of Liverpool. “A network of green and blue spaces, with the central park at the heart, now forms the backbone for our neighbourhoods. We understand better the assets that sit below the ground and the history on and above it – views old and new structure the place. “Hill Dickinson stadium changes the game; literally – for Everton Football Club and North Liverpool. It was never in the original masterplan [from 2013] and so we must adapt to respond to it and the opportunities it brings. Our wider variety of homes now represents a more inclusive, family-focused, inter-generational Liverpool Waters. “Today’s consent embodies Peel Waters’ future-facing attitude and commitment to the quality of buildings and their supporting infrastructure – to remake a place that will play a major role in North Liverpool’s sustainable future.” The approved masterplan retains Liverpool Waters’ five-neighbourhood structure comprising Princes Dock, KINGS, Central Docks, Clarence Docks and Northern Docks. Liverpool Waters also sits within the proposed Liverpool City Region Mayoral Development Zone, an initiative designed to accelerate regeneration, support investment and unlock the delivery of new homes, jobs and infrastructure. The approval of Peel Waters' updated masterplan represents the next stage in the evolution of Liverpool’s northern waterfront, building on the investment made by Everton in delivering Hill Dickinson Stadium and the Club’s longstanding ambition for its new home to be a driver of economic growth, regeneration and lasting opportunities for North Liverpool and the wider city region.

Liverpool City Council has approved an updated Liverpool Waters masterplan, marking another significant milestone in the regeneration of the city’s northern waterfront and building on the transformation brought about by the development of Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium.

The revised planning framework, brought forward by Peel Waters, will guide the next phase of development across the 60-hectare site stretching from Everton's headquarters at The Royal Liver Building to the Club’s new waterfront home at Bramley-Moore Dock.

The development of Hill Dickinson Stadium has acted as a catalyst for the regeneration of North Liverpool, stimulating investment, creating employment opportunities, attracting visitors and unlocking the potential of a previously underutilised area of the city.

The updated masterplan reflects the significant changes that have taken place along Liverpool’s waterfront since the original planning consent was granted in 2013, most notably the development of Everton’s latest home and its emergence as a major sporting, entertainment and visitor destination.

The refreshed prepares will support the delivery of latest homes, including affordable housing, alongside high-quality public spaces, healthcare provision, community facilities, employment opportunities and sustainable infrastructure across five distinctive waterfront neighbourhoods.

Central to the plans is the creation of a upcoming five-acre waterfront park at Central Docks. Already under construction as part of Liverpool Waters’ £81 million infrastructure investment programme, the park will feature more than 3,000 trees and is expected to open in spring 2028.

The park and wider development will provide new and enhanced pedestrian routes through the northern docks, offering supporters and visitors an optional attractive walking route between Liverpool city centre and Hill Dickinson Stadium.

Alongside newly introduced leisure and hospitality destinations, the creation of these public spaces will help transform the matchday and non-matchday journey for Evertonians, providing more opportunities for supporters to spend time along the waterfront before and after fixtures and major events at the stadium.

The increased focus on pedestrian connectivity, active travel and sustainable transport also complements Everton’s ongoing work with key stakeholders to improve accessibility to Hill Dickinson Stadium and better connect the Club’s waterfront home with the city centre and surrounding communities.

Colin Chong, Everton’s Chief Real Estate and Regeneration Officer, noted: “From the outset, our ambition for Hill Dickinson Stadium extended far beyond delivering a new home for Everton Football Club. It was also about unlocking the potential of Liverpool’s northern waterfront and providing a catalyst for wider investment, regeneration and economic growth.

“We are already seeing the positive impact of the stadium on the surrounding area, with upcoming businesses establishing themselves and existing businesses benefiting from increased footfall and activity.

“The updated Liverpool Waters masterplan provides an opportunity to build on that momentum. Newly introduced public spaces, improved walking routes and better connectivity will complement our own investment in establishing Hill Dickinson Stadium and our Budweiser Plaza as a year-round destination, enhancing the appeal of the area, attracting more visitors and creating further opportunities for businesses, investment and employment across North Liverpool.”.

The growing programme of major sporting and entertainment events at Hill Dickinson Stadium is extending the economic benefits of Everton’s investment beyond football matchdays and across the wider Liverpool City Region.

As well as being the home for Everton's Premier League fixtures, Hill Dickinson Stadium has already hosted an international football fixture between Scotland and Côte d’Ivoire, a Rugby League Ashes Test, Magic WKND and a Rugby Union Nations Championship fixture, the stadium will also host matches during UEFA EURO 2028, with a programme of major concerts at the Club’s waterfront home set to get under way in summer 2027.

The ability to attract events of national and international significance is helping to further strengthen Liverpool’s reputation as a global sporting, cultural and entertainment destination, drawing additional visitors to the city, supporting its hotel, hospitality, retail and transport sectors, and creating further opportunities for investment and employment across the region.

Since the original Liverpool Waters masterplan was approved in 2013, the northern waterfront has undergone significant change, with the delivery of new residential developments, transport infrastructure, leisure and hospitality destinations and public spaces, alongside Hill Dickinson Stadium and the Isle of Man Ferry Terminal.

Sources indicate that james Whittaker, Managing Director of Peel Waters, said: “The approval of the updated Liverpool Waters masterplan marks another major milestone in the transformation of Liverpool’s northern waterfront. Since the original masterplan was approved in 2013, we have delivered significant progress across the site, including newly introduced homes, public spaces, leisure destinations, major transport infrastructure and the new Everton Stadium, helping establish Liverpool Waters as one of the UK’s most ambitious regeneration projects.

In a recent development, “This updated framework reflects the considerable investment already made by Peel Waters and our partners, while providing the flexibility needed to respond to evolving market demand and future opportunities. With over £81 million of infrastructure investment committed at Central Docks, Princes Dock nearing completion and a clear vision for future neighbourhoods, Liverpool Waters is entering an exciting latest chapter that will continue to create homes, jobs, investment and opportunities for Liverpool and the wider city region.”.

The revised framework also strengthens commitments around sustainability, biodiversity, climate resilience and the preservation of Liverpool’s rich maritime heritage – principles that were central to the development of Everton’s waterfront home.

Pete Swift, CEO and Co-Founder, Planit – the landscape architecture, urban design and masterplanning studio who also worked as part of the team to deliver Everton's new home, added: “We are overjoyed at the approval, not just for the Peel Waters and Liverpool Waters team but for the communities of Liverpool.

“A network of green and blue spaces, with the central park at the heart, now forms the backbone for our neighbourhoods. We understand better the assets that sit below the ground and the history on and above it – views old and newly introduced structure the place.

“Hill Dickinson stadium changes the game; literally – for Everton Football Club and North Liverpool. It was never in the original masterplan [from 2013] and so we must adapt to respond to it and the opportunities it brings. Our wider variety of homes now represents a more inclusive, family-focused, inter-generational Liverpool Waters.

“Today’s consent embodies Peel Waters’ future-facing attitude and commitment to the quality of buildings and their supporting infrastructure – to remake a place that will play a major role in North Liverpool’s sustainable future.”.

The approved masterplan retains Liverpool Waters’ five-neighbourhood structure comprising Princes Dock, KINGS, Central Docks, Clarence Docks and Northern Docks.

Liverpool Waters also sits within the proposed Liverpool City Region Mayoral Development Zone, an initiative designed to accelerate regeneration, support investment and unlock the delivery of new homes, jobs and infrastructure.

The approval of Peel Waters' updated masterplan represents the next stage in the evolution of Liverpool’s northern waterfront, building on the investment made by Everton in delivering Hill Dickinson Stadium and the Club’s longstanding ambition for its upcoming home to be a driver of economic growth, regeneration and lasting opportunities for North Liverpool and the wider city region.

It kicks off at the Stadio Georgios Karaisakis in Piraeus at 17.45 GMT (18.45 CET).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from this game, Juventus-Omonia Nicosia and Borac-Atalanta on the Liveblog.

The Rossoneri might be doing well in Serie A, but their Europa League form has been appalling, losing three games without scoring a goal, making the 4-0 away to RB Salzburg an outlier.

Coach Ruben Amorim doesn’t even have the option of squad rotation today, because injuries ruled out Luka Modric, Francesco Camarda, Davide Bartesaghi, Strahinja Pavlovic, Samuel Chukwueze, Matteo Gabbia, Ruben Loftus-Cheek, Alexis Saelemaekers and Pietro Terracciano.

With all that in mind, Goncalo Ramos is allowed no rest, supported by Diego Moreira and Cisse, but potentially moving Hutchinson into a central trequartista role.

Mike Maignan returns from suspension after his red card against Bournemouth.

Milan have never won away to a Greek side in Europe, managing just four draws and two defeats, including a 3-1 loss to Olympiacos in December 2018.

Olympiacos are still unbeaten in the Europa League so far this season, beating Jagiellonia, Olympique Marseille and Sparta Prague before the 0-0 at Stade Rennais.

Notably, they conceded only one goal in those four games and sit in sixth place.

They too have a few injury problems, because former Roma flop Leon Bailey, Chiquinho, Gustavo Puerta and Santiago Hezze are out, plus long-term absentees and cup-tied Yusuf Yazici, Balsa Popovic, Ayoub El Kaabi, Marius Mouandilmadji, Clayton, Joel Roca and Lorenzo Scipioni.

Former Inter defender Lorenzo Pirola is starting, with ex-Torino midfielder Marcus Pedersen and former Bologna midfielder Remo Freuler in the side.

Olympiacos: Ortega; Retsos, Smajlovic, Pirola, Bruno Onyemaechi; Freuler Gustavo Sá; Pedersen, Joao Silva, Gelson Martins; Gonzalez.

Milan: Maignan; Gila, De Winter, Diawara, Estupinan; Jashari, Rabiot; Moreira, Cisse, Hutchinson; Ramos.

#140337. DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (950 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that you know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black?
  • Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?
  • Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that you know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black? It seems like it's not doing anything. But it's not doing nothing. It's syncing your messages, updating apps and running other background processes.

Your brain has its own version of that.

Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?

Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.

It's going over your memories, shaping your sense of who you are, imagining possible futures, helping you understand other people and connecting ideas.

That's your brain's default mode network.

Scientists conducted brain-imaging experiments in the 1990s and early 2000s to find out which regions of the brain were active during demanding tasks, like solving a math problem or memory exercise.

But to measure that, they needed a so-called baseline. They needed to know the level of brain activity at rest and during demanding tasks.

So, between the tasks, they asked participants to relax, close their eyes, stare at a fixed point on a wall, or try not to think of anything at all.

It has been revealed that and they measured the participants' brain activity both when they were solving a task and doing nothing. That's how scientists noticed the brain was active in up- and downtime.

It has been revealed that they noticed that when participants started to focus on a new task, after having done nothing, some brain areas lit up and other areas dimmed down. That suggests those areas that dimmed down must have been active while the participant was apparently — physically and mentally — at rest.

This realization eventually led to the discovery of the default mode network or DMN.

The DMN is crucial because it helps your brain make sense of your life and experiences.

It helps you connect and revisit memories, reflect on who you are, imagine what might happen in future scenarios, understand other people, build meaning from experience, and connect ideas in latest ways.

Recent findings suggest that it turns all your memories, experiences, knowledge, emotions and social information into your internal story. Think of that story as a constantly evolving, updated model of who you are and how you engage with the world around you.

Sources indicate that but it's important to understand the DMN involves more than one area of the brain. It is a group of brain regions that light up when you're not focused on an external task.

It has been revealed that there's another player in your brain that acts as a monitoring system. You can think of it as constantly asking "Is there anything that needs my attention?".

Imagine you're daydreaming while driving, and a car suddenly swerves into your lane.

In a fraction of a second, your daydream disappears and your attention snaps back to the road. That player is called the salience network, or SN.

The salience network helps you notice notable signals, like a sound, a mistake, pain, an emotion, a threat, or something happening in your body, and helps shift the brain toward attention and control systems when action is needed.

The DMN, SN and attention/control systems constantly interact.

Industry observers note that and the DMN doesn't just turn off completely with every hard task. Parts of it can also contribute when tasks involve memory, stories, meaning or other people.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Smartphones have filled many of the small empty moments of our days — waiting for the bus, standing in line, eating alone, lying on the couch. We are constantly looking at our devices.

So, it seems reasonable to ask: are we crowding out those moments of boredom where DMN kicks in?

Sources indicate that maybe. But so far, there's no strong evidence that scrolling directly affects mental health by reducing DMN time.

What we do know is that problematic smartphone use can increase stress, anxiety, task-switching and disrupt sleep.

And sleep loss and stress also have clearer evidence for altering DMN-related brain connectivity.

The DMN is not always necessarily good.

When your mind wanders, it might produce a great latest idea.

But it might also replay an embarrassing thing you did five years ago. Again. And again.

In depression, the self-reflection part of the DMN can get caught in repetitive negative loops that are hard to stop — what's known as rumination.

Industry observers note that scientists have also found that Alzheimer's disease targets key DMN areas, particularly those responsible for your autobiographical memory and remembering other aspects of the past. Which may help explain why memory problems are so central to the disease.

Sources indicate that protect your sleep and take stress seriously. There is direct evidence that sleep loss and stress disrupt DMN-related connectivity.

Take real, quiet breaks after mentally demanding tasks, like studying. It can even help you memorize facts for your exam.

Embrace boredom and enjoy doing nothing.

Try to reframe boredom as this essential, energy-intensive active work in your brain that builds your internal narrative and sense of self, consolidates memories, creates connections and sparks creativity.

It has been revealed that try waiting in line without checking your phone. Look out the window next time you take the bus or take a walk without listening to anything.

You can also try scheduling DMN time. It may be the closest thing to a real brain hack.

It has been revealed that this Christmas, a lifelong Evertonian is sharing how Everton in the Community helped him survive the loneliest time of his life after his wife died just 12 hours after the birth of their second son. Sean Foster, from Wigan, lost his wife Taylor in the early hours of 1 July 2020. Taylor was just 25 years old and passed away due to a splenic artery aneurysm, after being found unresponsive by staff on the mother and baby ward. Sean faced the devastating reality of raising two young children without his wife, while navigating grief, anxiety and suicidal thoughts. He noted: “I’ve been through grief before, but this was something else. “You’re not just grieving for the person you’ve lost; it’s the future you had with them, it’s what they’ll miss out on with the kids and what the kids will miss out on with having their mum. “With grief also came overwhelming struggles with PTSD, depression, anxiety and suicidal ideation. One thing that accompanies grief, which I have found the hardest and most persistent to cope with, is loneliness.”Just six days after Taylor's death, Sean reached out to Everton in the Community on Twitter (now X) in the middle of the night – a decision he described as his “hail Mary” and the first step towards seeking help. “My newborn baby and his two-year-old brother were asleep, and I found myself feeling completely alone, drowning in grief and crying uncontrollably. “It was a hail Mary. I just needed to reach out to someone and, as an Evertonian, I knew about Everton in the Community – but I didn’t expect the level of help I did get. It was a lifesaver.”  A donation to Everton in the Community this Christmas will help the official charity of Everton Football Club to support more people like Sean and to ensure no one has to face loneliness alone. Although Sean had immense support from friends and family, he didn’t want to worry them. He continued: “By lunchtime, I had a response from Everton in the Community and just a couple of hours after that I was on the phone with them. “The support I got from them was second to none and I know I would have found that period of my life so much harder if I hadn’t reached out.”Donate to Everton in the CommunityA member of Everton in the Community’s team visited Sean, providing essential items to help him care for his two young sons. The charity's wellbeing team also signposted him to additional organisations for grief support, while regular phone calls gave Sean someone to turn to during some of his most difficult moments. He also received support in navigating practical challenges, including his finances and helping his children understand what had happened. Sean received a call from Everton legend Duncan Ferguson on the day Taylor's cause of death was confirmed. Taking the time to ask Sean about his wife and what she was like, the conversation marked an important moment in his journey, helping him take the first steps towards talking about Taylor again. “Taylor was a force to be reckoned with,” Sean said. “She was genuinely one of a kind. A lot of people will say it about her, she was so thoughtful and she always looked out for others before herself. “Even the gifts she’d give on birthdays and Christmas, she’d know exactly what each person wanted and needed, make a care package, wrap it nicely and put a bow on it. “She was really into her arts and crafts and my eldest, he had two years with her, one of the things he always remembers is colouring with his mum.” Reflecting on the importance of having someone to turn to, Sean says he dreads to think about what might have happened had he not reached out to EitC. “I was in a really dark place and considering suicide," he admitted. "It’s not that I wanted to die. I wanted the kids to have a full family, a mum and dad figure and a safe, stable home. At that point in time I didn’t think I was giving them that. If I hadn’t reached out or got a response, I really struggle to think where I’d be.” Sean has since become an advocate for men’s mental health, including volunteering for Andy’s Man Club and starting his own podcast about grief. He has received therapy and attends group support sessions where he passionately talks about issues such as loneliness. He said: “The loneliest I have ever felt was at Christmas, the year Taylor died. All my family were crammed into my mum and dad's house, as we do every year, all 20-plus of us in the living room, scrambling to find our pile of presents as we did every year. “Only this year, Taylor wasn’t there laughing at the Christmas chaos. To this day I have never felt as lonely as I did in that moment.” Although he still experiences moments of loneliness, Sean says the support he has received has helped him understand that he doesn't have to face them alone. He hopes that by sharing his experience, he can encourage others who may be struggling to reach out, particularly during a time of year when feelings of loneliness can become more difficult. Sean said: “Loneliness isn’t the same as being alone. “We can have people around us, we can see friends, family, colleagues daily, but we can still feel lonely. “What I found about loneliness, particularly as a man, is that there's a stigma around talking about it, there's an expectation that we should just be strong, just get on with it and deal with it ourselves. “Most of the time that is the expectation we put on ourselves, when the fact is the real strength is in asking for help, admitting we might need a hand every now and then. “I still experience moments of loneliness, but they aren't as all-consuming. Thanks to Everton in the Community, I've learned I'm never truly alone.”  A donation to Everton in the Community this Christmas could help someone facing loneliness find the support they need – someone to listen and somewhere to turn when things feel impossible.

He hopes that by sharing his experience, he can encourage others who may be struggling to reach out, particularly during a time of year when feelings of loneliness can become more difficult.

Sean noted: “Loneliness isn’t the same as being alone.

“We can have people around us, we can see friends, family, colleagues daily, but we can still feel lonely.

“What I found about loneliness, particularly as a man, is that there's a stigma around talking about it, there's an expectation that we should just be strong, just get on with it and deal with it ourselves.

“Most of the time that is the expectation we put on ourselves, when the fact is the real strength is in asking for help, admitting we might need a hand every now and then.

Industry observers note that “I still experience moments of loneliness, but they aren't as all-consuming. Thanks to Everton in the Community, I've learned I'm never truly alone.”.

A donation to Everton in the Community this Christmas could help someone facing loneliness find the support they need – someone to listen and somewhere to turn when things feel impossible.
